entry.title: THE LEDGER SAID TWO THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED EIGHT TO NOUGHT — THE NINTH INNING SAID OTHERWISE: CINCINNATIS 10, BAY NINE 9
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 50 · Thursday, the Seven-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE LEDGER SAID TWO THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED EIGHT TO NOUGHT — THE NINTH INNING SAID OTHERWISE: CINCINNATIS 10, BAY NINE 9

Six runs in arrears with three outs left to their name, the Reds send eleven men to the plate against a franchise that in 2,208 previous trials had never once surrendered such a lead: the rookie Rodríguez opens the frame with a splash into McCovey Cove, Suárez — set upon the waiver wire by that very morning's report — answers with a grand slam, and the tying and winning runs arrive by bunt, theft, and sacrifice, the club's first such resurrection since 1958

In all the recorded history of the San Francisco franchise, the club had carried a lead of six runs or better into the ninth inning on two thousand two hundred eight occasions, and two thousand two hundred eight times it had come away the winner. That was the ledger the Cincinnatis consulted when they batted in the ninth at Oracle Park on Wednesday night, trailing nine runs to three — a deficit built while their starter Lodolo labored through four innings and Devers (his nine-and-twentieth homer), Cox and Whitcomb likewise clearing the fence, and Gilbert with three runs driven in feasted at their leisure. Cincinnati's manager Francona had spent Tuesday night in conference with his hitting counselors Benavides and Napoli before settling on a novelty: the two-and-twenty-year-old rookie Héctor Rodríguez, called up only this fourth of August, would bat leadoff — ahead of De La Cruz — and the experiment survived even San Francisco's late announcement, three hours before the first pitch, that the ace Webb had been moved up to oppose him. Rodríguez tied the game once already with a homer in the third; the ledger, as noted, was unimpressed.

Then came the ninth, and the ledger was burned. Rodríguez opened it with a blast over the right-field wall struck at 115 miles to the hour, a drive of some 423 feet that did not stop at the seats but found the waters of McCovey Cove itself — just the third splash hit ever authored by a Cincinnati man, and the first since Votto and Moustakas managed it on consecutive days in April of 2021. "That big homer by Héctor woke us up in the dugout," testified Eugenio Suárez — and here the morning's cruelest irony bears telling, for the wires had reported only that day that Suárez and his clubmate Friedl were placed on waivers, as the dealings desk relates below. The reliever Bivens filled the bases without recording an out, whereupon the waived man deposited a grand slam into the left-center seats, his nineteenth homer, and nine-to-three had become nine-to-eight. The rest was deadball chapter and verse: Myers beat out a bunt and advanced on the throw gone astray, McLain bunted for another single, stole second, and took third as Trevino's sacrifice fly leveled the account, and the pinch-hitter Stephenson lined the go-ahead single to left. Pagán closed the door on his seventeenth save; the win fell to Santillan, the loss to the unfortunate Smith, now nought-and-five.

Eleven men to the plate, seven runs across, and a page of history rewritten: the researchers certify it just the third victory in all the Reds' annals when trailing by six or more entering the ninth — and by some prank of the almanac both predecessors fell upon the eighth of May, one in 1918 at St. Louis, the other in 1958 at Chicago. Nor was the evening's only century concern the ledger's: Sal Stewart's sacrifice fly in the seventh, modest freight at the time, carried the rookie to one hundred runs batted in, of which the milestone desk sings below. Cincinnati stands but three-and-sixty wins against one-and-seventy defeats, and the pennant tables will scarcely notice; but a three-game skid is snapped, and the annals will remember this one long after the standings have forgotten the year.

News Around the League

THE DEALINGS DESK: CINCINNATI SETS SUÁREZ AND FRIEDL UPON THE WAIVER WIRE — AND SUÁREZ ANSWERS WITH A GRAND SLAM BY NIGHTFALL

The wires report — the account issuing from Rosenthal of The Athletic, the club itself declining to confirm — that the Reds have placed the veteran slugger Eugenio Suárez and the outfielder TJ Friedl on waivers, opening a window of eight-and-forty hours in which any of the other nine-and-twenty clubs may claim either man. Suárez, five-and-thirty years of age, returned to Cincinnati on a one-year engagement of fifteen millions after eight seasons there earlier in his career, and has struggled to a .705 mark by the OPS ledger across 103 games — though the reader of the lead column knows what he did Wednesday night with the waiver wire fresh about his shoulders, and his nineteenth homer of the year was no modest one. Friedl's season has run crueler still: a .476 OPS across six-and-seventy games, lowest among the 274 batsmen with two hundred fifty trips to the plate, and a June spent largely in the minors — a far cry from the .742 he posted only last season. The Herald observes that the waiver wire has rarely received a man on the very evening of his grandest swing, and awaits the claiming clubs' verdict with interest.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: SASAKI'S FINGER BETRAYS HIM IN ATLANTA, THE FIFTEEN-DAY LIST BECKONS, AND THE UNICORN'S RETURN DRAWS NEARER STILL

The Los Angeles rotation, so lately restored to nearly full strength, is short a man again. Roki Sasaki departed Wednesday's engagement at Atlanta in the fourth inning, undone by a blister upon his right middle finger — "My skin just ripped off, and then after that, it got worse," the four-and-twenty-year-old related through his interpreter — and his manager Roberts pronounced the sentence afterward: the fifteen-day injured list, there being, in the manager's words, no way to avoid it given the severity. Sasaki was charged four runs on six hits across three and one-third innings, an abrupt halt to a stretch in which he had pitched to a 2.31 earned-run figure over six starts; the left-hander Lauer stands in position to take his turn. The ward notes the fuller accounting: Glasnow returned Tuesday, Snell on the eleventh of August, and Shohei Ohtani — whose progress toward the mound this paper has tracked since the four-and-twentieth — is expected to rejoin the rotation within the week. The unicorn paws at the gate yet.

THE MILESTONE DESK: STEWART'S HUNDRED ARRIVES ON A SACRIFICE FLY, SCHWARBER IS FIRST OF ALL BASEBALL TO FORTY, AND ALONSO DRAWS LEVEL WITH ALVAREZ'S CROWN

Three vigils this desk has kept all week, and two of them ended in a single evening. Sal Stewart of Cincinnati, one stroke shy when yesterday's paper went to press, lifted a bases-loaded sacrifice fly in the seventh at San Francisco and became a man of one hundred runs batted in — master of all baseball's table, the Cardinal pair Burleson and Walker trailing at eight-and-ninety and seven-and-ninety after their own six-run fifth in defeat, as the card relates — with the rookie's larger distinction, a runs-batted-in title unclaimed by any freshman since 1950, still there for the seizing. In Seattle, Kyle Schwarber struck a three-run blast off Woo in the second inning, his fortieth of the season and the first fortieth in either league this year: a fourth forty-homer campaign in five Philadelphia summers, drawing him level with Ryan Howard for the most in that franchise's history, and level besides with Ohtani and Judge for the most among all men now active. And in the American, the crown of three this paper has chronicled upon Yordan Alvarez's brow is besieged at one corner: Pete Alonso of the Orioles drove home two at St. Louis, his two-and-thirtieth homer among them, and stands level with the idle-handed Houston colossus at one-and-ninety runs batted in apiece — though Alvarez holds the batting table at .322 and the homer column at six-and-thirty, with Caminero and Rice a single blast astern at five-and-thirty.

THE RECORDS DESK: FIVE EVENINGS, FIVE HOME RUNS — PETERS JOINS THE WHITE STOCKINGS' PANTHEON, AND NO CLUB SINCE 1900 HAS RAISED TWO SUCH ROOKIES IN ONE SUMMER

The watch this desk posted two mornings ago is concluded: Tristan Peters, the White Stockings' rookie left fielder, homered for a fifth consecutive game Wednesday — a two-run blast off the Texas reliever Ahlstrom in the sixth, and the first homer of his major-league life struck off a left-hander — to draw level with the franchise record, a summit shared by seven men across eight prior occasions, among them Frank Thomas twice in 1994, Kittle, Luzinski, and his own clubmate Murakami earlier this very season. Five straight likewise ties the longest streak ever fashioned by a rookie, and the researchers at Elias certify the stranger distinction: no club since at least 1900 had ever raised two rookies to a home-run streak of five games in a single summer until the South Side managed it twice in one. The all-time mark of eight, held by Griffey Jr., Mattingly, and Dale Long, now sits three evenings distant. "That's crazy," the author allowed. The arithmetic behind the fireworks: since the eighth of August, Peters is batting .400 with six homers across eighteen games — and for a second consecutive victory he finished a triple shy of the cycle.

THE ALMANAC DESK: SKUBAL IS APPOINTED FOR COMERICA PARK ON FRIDAY, WHERE THE TIGERS WILL BEHOLD THEIR OWN LATE ACE IN VISITING FLANNELS

The schedule, consulted and confirmed, offers Friday evening a reunion of rare theater: the Dodgers open their weekend engagement at Detroit at 6:40 by the Eastern clock, and Los Angeles has announced that Tarik Skubal — winner of consecutive American League Cy Young Awards in 2024 and 2025, all of it in Detroit flannels — will take the Comerica Park mound against the club that raised him, for the first time since the blockbuster that carried him west before the third-of-August deadline. The southpaw has pitched to a 3.38 earned-run figure across four Los Angeles starts, striking out thirty against seven walks, and collected his first victory in the new livery on Saturday last with eleven strikeouts against Pittsburgh. Of the parting he has said the emotions ran a rollercoaster — "The goal was always to win a World Series for the city" — and the Herald expects Comerica's reception Friday to say the rest.

The Rest of the Card

THE COLLISION'S SECOND ACT GOES TO THE HOME NINE AT THE LAST SWING: KIM, HITLESS SINCE JUNE, SINGLES HOME THE VERDICT — PEACHTREE NINE 6, BOYS IN BLUE 5

The heavyweight engagement between the National's two grandest records produced a second straight one-run verdict for Atlanta, and an ending no dramatist would have dared submit. Level at five apiece in the ninth — Edman having driven home three for the visitors and homered his fifth, Olson's seven-and-thirtieth and the catcher Murphy's first anchoring the home ledger — the home nine put the winning run aboard with two out and sent up Ha-Seong Kim, a man without a base hit since the third of June, owner of an 0-for-27 famine, a .068 opening act across his first seven-and-twenty games, and a twenty-million-dollar salary lately whispered of as sunk cost. Kim ran the count to three-and-nought against the closer Scott, took a called strike, spoiled three further offerings, and laced a 97-mile four-seamer to left for the walk-off — his first hit in nearly three months, and the sweetest of his American life. The win fell to Mederos, the loss to Scott, now one-and-five; Sasaki's early exit is the ward's business above. Atlanta has won three running; the third act goes this very evening at 7:15, Yamamoto opposing Sale — Sale and Yamamoto owning the National's second- and fourth-best earned-run figures respectively, and one box score to share between them.

A CORRECTION ADMINISTERED IN THE BRONX, AND THE CROWN QUESTION HOLDS: PINSTRIPES 9, SPACE CITY NINE 3

New York settled Wednesday's business early and thoroughly: Rice struck his five-and-thirtieth homer — drawing level with Caminero, one behind Alvarez's American lead — while García Jr. added his eight-and-twentieth with two driven in, and Bellinger chipped in a pair of his own as nine runs crossed against three in reply. Blackburn, whose work this paper commended only Monday against Toronto, ran his ledger to six-and-two; Sousa bore the Houston loss. Varsho's tenth homer and Altuve's double were the visitors' consolation, and the arithmetic holds its breath: with Texas also beaten, Houston keeps the West's crown by the same half game, the finale of the set appointed for 7:05 this evening with Cole opposing Wesneski.

PERALTA, TWICE TRADED AND LONG SUFFERING, FINDS HIS FASTBALL AT COMERICA: SUNSHINE NINE 3, BENGALS 0

Freddy Peralta — dealt by Milwaukee to the Mets in January, dealt again to Tampa Bay on the second of August, and carrying a sorrowful five-and-eleven ledger into the afternoon — pitched six scoreless innings on two hits with nary a walk for his first victory in his newest flannels, looking every inch the man who won seventeen a season ago. The Bengals' entire offense was two opposite-field singles, by Dingler and Callahan; Kelly and Wells (his fifth save) closed the whitewash. Hicks drove home a run, DeLuca doubled home another, and Mullins cashed the third, and the rubber game broke Tampa Bay's season-high run of three consecutive series lost. The league leaders thus hold the East by three games and a half over the Bronx; the Bengals surrender the set a day after Clark's heroics graced these pages.

RODRIGUEZ OUTDUELS BOYD, AND THE BALK THAT WASN'T DECIDES WHAT THE BATS COULD NOT: SNAKES 2, BRUINS 0

A proper pitchers' argument in the desert — Eduardo Rodriguez running his ledger to fourteen-and-four against Boyd's dazzling eight innings' work — turned on a call not made. With Crow-Armstrong at third in the sixth, Rodriguez appeared to step off the rubber mid-windup as the runner broke for home; no balk was called, the play being beyond review's reach, and the crew chief Márquez confessed afterward that one should have been. Chicago stranded its man, whereupon Lawlar homered in the bottom half, his third, and Waldschmidt — Tuesday's midnight hero in these pages — drove home the insurance. Two hits the whole evening for the Bruins, Morillo sealing the second save. The Snakes take the rubber match and draw within a single game of San Diego for the National's last chair; the Cubs, their cushion in the wild-card row still four games, will want the memory of this trip burned.

TWICE IN TWO NIGHTS THE NINTH BELONGS TO CLEVELAND: FOREST CITY NINE 4, ANGELS 3, AND THE STREAK RUNS TO SEVEN

One evening after Ramírez's three-double resurrection graced these pages, the Forest City men did it again: trailing three-to-two with but two outs remaining, they summoned DeLauter — kept from the starting lineup a third straight day by a balky left hamstring — and he promptly singled the tying run aboard. Two runs crossed before the inning closed, Bazzana driving home a pair on the night and Kwan and Lowe the rest, and Sabrowski recorded his first save behind the winner Gaddis. The particulars beggar belief: Anaheim managed but three hits and still nearly won; Cleveland has taken seven running, matching its season best, swept the set, and closed a road expedition six victories to none. The final wild-card chair is theirs by two full games over Texas, with the Central's summit but two and a half distant — and the Herald reminds the reader that this same club sat level at the break-even line only Tuesday morning.

SCHWARBER'S FORTIETH ANCHORS A SIX-RUN ARGUMENT BY THE SOUND: PHILS 6, SEATTLE MEN 0

The Philadelphias, twice beaten in this yard since their nine-game streak perished, salvaged the finale emphatically: two runs in the first, four in the second — Schwarber's three-run fortieth, the milestone desk's business above, and Harper's seven-and-twentieth in close company — and Luzardo did the rest, running his ledger to twelve-and-five with Seattle held to two hits entire. Woo absorbed the damage. The Phils hold the National's second wild-card chair at two games' cushion and depart for Anaheim; Seattle, blanked at home, remains in the thick of nothing so much as its own frustrations.

A SHUTOUT FROM THE SHORTHANDED: SAN DIEGO NINE 3, ALLEGHENYS 0

With the bullpen chieftains Miller and Morejon both unavailable, the San Diego relief corps followed Vásquez — ten victories now against six defeats — through a whitewash of Pittsburgh, the rookie Chandler taking the loss and Rodriguez sealing the second save. Merrill supplied a triple and a double and drove home a run, Cronenworth and Rengifo the others, and the Alleghenys' five hits included Gonzales's evening at shortstop marred by his fifteenth error. The Friars' grip on the National's last chair thus survives the desert's gains: one game, no more, as the card above relates.

FOUR ERRORS, NO RUNS, AND THE STREAK DIES AT FIVE: FISH 4, CRIMSON HOSE 0

Boston's five-game run of victories perished by its own hand at Miami: four errors — two apiece by Sogard and Wong — behind Gray, the American's leader in victories, who fell to sixteen-and-four despite modest damage of the earned variety. The Fish needed no more: Sanoja stole three bases and drove home a run, Hernández cashed another and swiped his ninth, and Gusto claimed his first victory of the season with the shutout's lion's share. Miami's home fortress now reads two-and-forty wins against seven-and-twenty defeats — and the Fish, quietly, sit four games from the National's last chair.

THE THIRTEEN COMES BACK WITH THE RECEIPT: COLORADANS 13, WASHINGTONS 1

On Monday the Washingtons dealt Colorado a thirteen-to-three drubbing; Wednesday the Coloradans returned the identical thirteen and kept the change. Four runs in the fifth, four in the seventh, five in the eighth — Goodman's six-and-thirtieth homer leading a quartet that included Carrigg, Norby, and Johnston, with Norby driving home five by himself — and the left-hander Gordon collected his first victory of the season. Chaparro's ninth homer was the Capital's lone reply. Two straight now for the visitors since the Monday humiliation, with the set's finale at 1:05 this afternoon; the Washingtons have lost eight of their last ten.

LUKES SETTLES TUESDAY'S DEBT WITH INTEREST: TORONTOS 3, KANSAS CITY NINE 0, AND THE ROYAL STREAK DIES AT NINE

The reader will recall Tuesday's ending in Toronto: Lukes cut down at second base by telegraph relay, the final out of a Kansas City victory. Wednesday the same man wrote the correction — a three-run homer, his ninth, all the scoring the Torontos required — while Dallas and the relief corps blanked the hottest club in the land on six hits, Varland sealing his thirtieth save. So perishes the Royal winning streak at nine, their longest since 2017, with Dobnak the hard-luck loser; the two nines conclude the series at 7:07 this evening. The Herald notes that redemption, like the post, is most satisfying delivered to the same address.

ONE PITCH FOR MAY, SIX SINGLES IN FILE, AND A SQUIRREL UPON THE NETTING: MILWAUKEES 8, METS 1

The evening at Citi Field began alarmingly: Dustin May's first and only pitch came screaming back off Ewing's bat at 106 miles to the hour and struck the pitcher, ending his night at once on a day the Milwaukee bullpen was already thin — the second day, no less, of sixteen games in sixteen days. Whereupon the best record in baseball showed its manners: Gasser supplied the better part of six innings' emergency relief for the win, and the second inning opened with six consecutive singles — the club's first such inning since 1998 — before Turang's seventeenth homer, his first since July, fattened the account to eight. Frelick, restored from his shoulder trouble, collected three hits. The proceedings were interrupted in the third by a squirrel descending the protective netting, which the Herald records as the evening's only Met to reach the field with intent. Milwaukee stands two-and-eighty wins against one-and-fifty defeats; the rematch this evening sends Misiorowski — sovereign of the National's earned-run table at 1.68 and its strikeout table at two hundred sixteen — against Manaea at 7:10.

THE ROOKIES CARRY THE SOUTH SIDE AGAIN: WHITE STOCKINGS 10, RANGERS 4

Beyond Peters's fifth consecutive blast — the records desk above has the full accounting — the South Side's evening ran deep: the catcher Doyle drove home four with his third homer, Peters himself finished with two driven in and stood a triple from the cycle, and Meidroth, Montgomery, and Acuña kept the doubles coming while Newcomb took the decision and Cannon his first save. For Texas, Pederson — lately ejected in these pages for quarreling with the automated arbiter — homered his three-and-twentieth in a losing cause, and Gore fell to seven-and-ten. The White Stockings hold the Central by two games and a half over surging Cleveland; the Rangers slip two astern of the wild-card row's last chair and half a game off the West's crown, a position best described as within sight of everything and in possession of nothing.

SEVEN RUNS IN TWO INNINGS, SIX GIVEN BACK IN ONE, AND THE NINTH DECIDES: ORIOLES 8, GAS HOUSE NINE 7

Baltimore struck five runs in the first and two in the second and appeared bound for a stroll; St. Louis answered with six in the fifth — Burleson and Walker driving home their eight-and-ninetieth and seven-and-ninetieth in the uprising, Church and Fermín and Gorman's eighth homer filling out the bill — and the affair arrived at the ninth level at seven. There the Orioles scratched the deciding run against O'Brien, the National's keeper of three-and-thirty saves, who thus absorbs his second late-inning calamity of the week in these pages. Alonso's two-and-thirtieth homer and two runs driven in carried him level with Alvarez atop the American's table, as the milestone desk relates; Taveras drove home three, Encarnacion-Strand doubled twice, and Kittredge sealed the seventh save behind Wolfram. Five straight defeats now for St. Louis, with the set concluding at 2:15 this afternoon.

THREE HOMERS ANSWERED BY ONE, AND THE ELEPHANTS' MARCH CONTINUES: A'S 7, MINNESOTANS 4

Minnesota did its scoring by the long ball — Lee's one-and-twentieth, Larnach's eleventh, the rookie Culpepper's third — and lost the argument anyway, Sacramento assembling seven runs behind Butler's twelfth homer, Williams's triple and two driven in, and small commerce from McNeil and Stefanic. Ginn pitched to his ninth victory, Morris took the loss, and Alvarado closed his fifth save. Two straight now for the A's, who play the spoiler with evident relish; for the Minnesotans, six games below the break-even line and slipping, the wild-card row recedes further from view.

With this number the Herald's ledger turns fifty editions old, and the arithmetic desk marks the occasion with a morning of settled furniture and unsettled margins. In the American: Tampa Bay holds the East by three games and a half; the White Stockings keep the Central by two and a half over a Cleveland club that has won seven running and owns the last wild-card chair by two full games over Texas, with Baltimore two and a half astern and Toronto three; and the West's half-game crown rests upon Houston's brow a second consecutive morning — a stillness itself remarkable, the same crown having changed heads three times in the three mornings prior. In the National the chairs hold: Chicago's cushion four games, Philadelphia's two, San Diego's last seat now but a single game ahead of Arizona with Miami four back, while Milwaukee's two-and-eighty victories remain the game's best. This evening's card runs to seven engagements, all verified against the schedule: the Coloradans and Washingtons settle accounts at 1:05, the Orioles and Cardinals at 2:15, Cole opposes Wesneski in the Bronx at 7:05, the Royals seek a new streak in Toronto at 7:07, Misiorowski carries his 1.68 into Flushing at 7:10, the collision's third act goes at Atlanta at 7:15 with Yamamoto opposing Sale, and the Snakes visit the Bay nine at 9:45 — where, after Wednesday's ninth inning, no lead in San Francisco will be presumed safe again. Friday brings Skubal to Comerica Park, as the almanac desk relates. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: SIXTEEN INNINGS OF FAMINE, THEN A FEAST AT THE STROKE OF MIDNIGHT: WALDSCHMIDT, SUMMONED FROM THE BENCH, ENDS IT WITH ONE SWING — ARIZONAS 5, NORTH SIDERS 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 49 · Wednesday, the Six-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIXTEEN INNINGS OF FAMINE, THEN A FEAST AT THE STROKE OF MIDNIGHT: WALDSCHMIDT, SUMMONED FROM THE BENCH, ENDS IT WITH ONE SWING — ARIZONAS 5, NORTH SIDERS 4

Four runs in arrears entering the eighth, without a tally in two evenings, the Sonoran nine collect three against the Chicago bullpen and then send a rookie to the plate cold — whose two-run blast wins the game, draws Arizona within a single game of the National's last chair, and closes the strangest day of Torey Lovullo's summer

For sixteen consecutive innings the Arizona bats had gone without a run — nine of them in Monday's shutout, chronicled in these pages, and seven more on Tuesday evening while the North Siders' Holmes spun a spell of his own: seven innings, two hits allowed, five strikeouts, and not a Phoenix runner permitted past his post. The visitors, meanwhile, had banked their evening early — Happ's three-run blast in the fourth, his three-and-twentieth, and a Busch single in the sixth had the ledger four to none, and the desert crowd had every reason to expect a second consecutive famine.

Then Holmes departed, and the spell went with him. In the eighth, against the reliever Palencia, Moreno doubled home a run and Perdomo singled home two more, and four-to-none had become four-to-three inside a quarter hour. In the ninth, with Fernandez aboard and the pitcher Webb on the hill, Lovullo turned to his bench — and here the manager confessed afterward to a comedy worthy of the vaudeville stage. Twice he asked his hitting men, Mather, Easley, and Denker, whom to send; twice they begged another minute's deliberation; at the last they pronounced their verdict: send Waldy. Ryan Waldschmidt, the rookie, batting for Barrosa with the game moving as Lovullo put it at warp speed, took his instructions, stepped cold to the plate, and deposited a two-run blast into the seats — his third home run of the season.

So ended a day Arizona will not soon forget: begun with its manager tendering an apology to his opposite number (the protocol desk relates the particulars below), and concluded with five runs in its final six outs against a club six games clear of it in the standings. The arithmetic is the sweetest part — the Sonoran nine now stand a single game behind San Diego for the National's final wild-card chair, and the two clubs' fortunes turned on the same midnight hour, as the rest of the card relates.

News Around the League

THE PROTOCOL DESK: LOVULLO TENDERS AN APOLOGY, AND THE LEAGUE PRONOUNCES THE SPYGLASS LAWFUL WHEN WORKED FROM SECOND BASE

The shouting that enlivened Monday's contest in Phoenix has ended in a handshake. The reader will recall that during Arizona's seven-to-none defeat, the Diamondbacks' bench took loud exception to the Cubs' third-base coach Quinton Berry, who was observed relaying to Chicago runners at second base when the Arizona starter Kelly meant to throw his changeup — the runner then wiring the intelligence onward to the batsman. Manager Torey Lovullo, his pitching coach Kaplan, and his bench coach Banister hollered at Berry to knock it off; Chicago's bench coach Flaherty hollered back; and a fine cross-field row was had by all. Lovullo, believing a rule forbade such traffic, carried the question to Michael Hill, the league's senior vice president of on-field operations, and received his answer Tuesday: there is no such rule. Espionage conducted in plain view from the bag is honest labor, as it has been since the deadball days, and the remedy — as every catcher of the old school knew — is to change the signs, not to petition the authorities. Lovullo, to his credit, took the ruling like a sportsman and conveyed his apology to Craig Counsell. That evening Arizona beat Chicago anyway, by means entirely above board, as the lead column attests.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: JUDGE GRADUATES FROM THE TEE TO LIVING PITCHING, SCHMIDT PLOTS A RETURN BY WAY OF THE BULLPEN, AND BUXTON'S HIP SOUNDS ITS ALARM ONCE MORE

From the Bronx, encouraging bulletins: Aaron Judge, whose confinement to the batting tee this paper noted Monday, on Tuesday took his swings against overhand pitching in the indoor cages beneath Yankee Stadium — the first such since his right rib began mending — and ran the outfield besides, his throwing now stretched to a hundred feet. His manager Boone, nodding toward the dugout stairs, offered the medical opinion of the age: he looks good. In the same camp, Clarke Schmidt faced hitters in a live session and stands close to a rehabilitation assignment, the club minded to return him by way of the bullpen for the stretch drive.

The news runs darker in Minnesota, where Byron Buxton departed Tuesday's contest in the seventh inning after chasing a line drive into the right-center gap and pulling up in evident discomfort. The complaint is the familiar one — the right hip that has troubled him since May and twice lodged him on the injured list — and the deceleration required of an outfielder in full flight remains its cruelest test. He is to be examined again Wednesday, and the Twins hold their breath.

THE MILESTONE DESK: STEWART STANDS ONE SHY OF A HUNDRED, ALONSO GATHERS FOUR HITS IN PURSUIT, PETERS STALKS A CLUB RECORD, AND THE CROWN OF THREE GROWS HEAVIER

The hundred-mark watch narrows to a single tally. Sal Stewart of Cincinnati, who stood two short when yesterday's paper went to press, homered in the ninth inning at San Francisco — his eight-and-twentieth — and now sits at nine-and-ninety runs batted in, one stroke from the century. The Cardinal pair who lurk behind him, Burleson and Walker, were held at six-and-ninety apiece by an evening in which their entire club managed one run. In the American, Pete Alonso of the Baltimores put up four hits and four runs batted in at St. Louis, his one-and-thirtieth homer among them, and stands at nine-and-eighty — second in the league's table, now but two tallies behind Yordan Alvarez, whose crown of three grows heavier by the morning: the Houston colossus tripled and drove in his one-and-ninetieth in the Bronx, and leads the American in average at .323, in home runs at six-and-thirty, and in runs batted in, all at once. And on the South Side, the rookie Tristan Peters has now homered in four consecutive games — one shy of the club record of five, set by his own teammate Murakami earlier this summer — of which feat the rest of the card has more to say.

THE ANNALS DESK: NINE PITCHES, THREE VICTIMS — BRADLEY WRITES A PAGE NO TWIN HAD WRITTEN BEFORE

In the fifth inning at Sacramento's grounds Tuesday night, Taj Bradley of the Twins accomplished what no Minnesota pitcher is known to have accomplished in the franchise's long and pitching-proud annals: the immaculate inning — three batsmen retired on strikes, nine pitches, not one wasted. Cortes went down swinging at a splitter that dove beneath the zone; Serven chased a curveball to the same fate; and Bolte, the leadoff man, was frozen by a fastball of 99.8 miles per hour laid on the black at the bottom of the zone. The catcher Caratini confessed afterward that he called the final fastball simply because it was the best pitch, and history could look after itself. That the feat came in a losing cause — the Athletics took the game, four to two — is the sort of joke the pastime reserves for its finest single innings, and the Herald records it here so the annals need not blush.

THE WILLIAMSPORT DESK: MISS RASMUS OF ALABAMA REWRITES THE GIRLS' LEDGER

From South Williamsport, where this paper's attentions lingered all weekend, word of a legend still growing: Kinley Rasmus, the twelve-year-old two-way player out of Phenix City, Alabama — daughter of the former big-league pitcher Cory Rasmus and niece of the outfielder Colby — has set a new record for hits by a girl in the Little League World Series, five and counting, as her nine pulled out a four-to-two victory over the Soundview club of Tacoma to advance toward the tournament's final stages. This on the heels of Monday's work, when she tied Mo'ne Davis's mark of fourteen strikeouts, the most ever recorded by a girl in the Series — the pair of them numbering among just nine girls ever to take the hill at Williamsport. The Herald tips its cap, and suspects it will not be the last time it sets her name in type.

The Rest of the Card

THE APPOINTMENT BY THE PACIFIC IS KEPT: SKENES SPOTLESS THROUGH SIX, KING MATCHES HIM SEVEN, AND CRUZ SETTLES IT IN THE NINTH — BUCS 1, FRIARS 0

This desk directed all eyes to San Diego at Tuesday's close, and the evening repaid the fare. Paul Skenes, whose recent labors had gone unrewarded, surrendered a leadoff double to Tatis on an oh-and-two pitch — a drive measured at 110 miles to the hour — and then nothing whatever: six scoreless innings, three hits, four strikeouts, not a walk, his first spotless start since the twelfth of May. San Diego's King answered with seven blank innings of his own, and the game arrived at the ninth a double cipher — whereupon Oneil Cruz lined his seventeenth home run off the closer Miller for the only run of the night. Montgomery locked the door for his sixth save, the Friars were held to three hits entire, and the Missions have now dropped two one-run decisions running to Pittsburgh — with Arizona, as the lead column relates, drawn to within a single game of their chair.

FIVE RUNS DOWN IN ANAHEIM, AND RAMÍREZ DECLINES THE VERDICT: CLEVELAND NINE 8, ANAHEIM NINE 6, IN TEN INNINGS

The Cleveland nine trailed five to none after two innings — a two-run Grissom homer, a Moore blast, and small-arms fire besides — and a lesser club would have consulted the timetable for the morning train. Instead: José Ramírez, vintage issue — three doubles on the night, five runs batted in: the two-run double in the fourth that began the climb, the equalizing double in the eighth after Grissom's second blast had restored the Anaheim lead, and at last the two-run double in the tenth that decided it. It stands as Cleveland's largest comeback of the season and their first from four or more runs down since August of last year; manager Vogt pronounced the affair a heart-pumper, which the Herald certifies as clinically accurate. The streak runs to six, Smith collected his five-and-thirtieth save, and the final wild-card chair remains Cleveland property for another morning.

NINE RUNNING, AND THE LAST OUT MADE BY TELEGRAPH RELAY: MISSOURIANS 5, CANADIANS 3

The hottest club in the land carried its business abroad and never broke stride. Lugo gave five innings of one-run ball, Salvador Perez supplied the go-ahead single in the fifth, and the veteran Scherzer — now one-and-seven on his sorrowful ledger — absorbed the defeat. Toronto made it interesting with two in the ninth, whereupon the game ended as prettily as any this season: Lukes's two-out knock into the gap was cut off by Collins, wired to Witt, and forwarded to Tolbert at second base, where Lukes was tagged out attempting his advance — a nine-game winning streak sealed by relay post. It is Kansas City's longest run since 2017, and no club in either league is presently hotter.

GASPER STRIKES TWICE, AND DURAN EMPTIES THE BASES IN THE ELEVENTH: HUB NINE 7, FLORIDIANS 3

A close-run affair ran long and then burst. Mickey Gasper homered twice in solo fashion, Miami answered each time, and the clubs traded single tallies again in the tenth — Boston's on a passed ball, the Floridians' on a wild pitch loosed even as the batsman struck out, which is the sort of bookkeeping that keeps official scorers honest. In the eleventh the Hub nine loaded the bases and Jarren Duran cleared them entirely, a grand slam to right-center — his eighteenth homer, four runs batted in — and the count of consecutive Boston victories runs to five, the win to the reliever Gamboa.

THE WEST'S CROWN CHANGES HEADS A THIRD MORNING RUNNING: ASTROS 9, AMERICANS 7, IN THE BRONX

A proper slugging match, thrice tied and turned about as often. Yainer Diaz struck two home runs, the second the equalizer in the eighth, whereupon Yordan Alvarez — the crown of three upon his brow — lashed a triple to put Houston in front and Paredes singled him home for margin. García Jr. homered, doubled, and drove in three for the Americans, and Chisholm brought them within one, but Diaz's single in the ninth restored the cushion and Hader closed the accounts for his nineteenth save. The arithmetic: Houston, at the break-even line of six-and-sixty apiece and with Espada restored to the bench as this paper related only yesterday, reclaims sole possession of the West's crown by half a game over Texas — the third different head to wear it in three mornings.

PETERS MAKES IT FOUR EVENINGS RUNNING, AND THE FIRST INNING DOES THE REST: SOUTH SIDERS 11, TEXAS NINE 7

Six runs in the opening frame off deGrom settled the general question, leaving only the particulars. Chief among them: the rookie Tristan Peters, late of the barnstorming Savannah Bananas, who doubled home two in that first-inning cannonade and later homered — his fourth consecutive game with a home run, a big evening at the plate that left him flirting with the cycle, and now one game shy of the club record of five straight as the milestone desk relates. Antonacci tripled and Vargas and the Montgomerys kept the queue moving; for Texas, Foscue and Burger and Jansen all homered in a losing cause. The Rangers thereby surrender the West's crown they had held for a single day.

EIGHT IN THE FIFTH AND NO MERCY IN MOUND CITY: BIRDS 13, REDBIRDS 1

The Baltimores fell upon St. Louis with a violence rarely seen outside the prize ring. Pete Alonso had four hits inside five innings — a three-run homer, his one-and-thirtieth, among them — and four runs batted in; Encarnacion-Strand homered and drove home three; and the fifth inning alone produced eight Baltimore runs, a parade to the plate that the St. Louis bullpen will see in its sleep. Bassitt cruised to the win, Church's homer supplied the Cardinal run, and St. Louis has now dropped four straight — their hundred-watch pair, as noted above, going hungry.

THREE AT THE FIRST KNOCK, ONE AT THE LAST: TOMAHAWK NINE 4, DODGERS 3

Atlanta greeted Glasnow, making his first start since May, with three first-inning runs — Dubón and Harris singling home a pair and Albies adding a sacrifice fly — though the big right-hander steadied thereafter and the champions drew level by the fourth on singles by Thomas, Feduccia, and Call. There matters stood until the eighth, when Ozzie Albies singled home Olson with the run that decided it; Iglesias closed for his eight-and-twentieth save. A heavyweight engagement between the National's two best records, taken by the home club — and the two nines are appointed to resume hostilities this very evening.

LINDOR SAVES IT WITH THE LEATHER, WINS IT WITH HIS LEGS: METROPOLITANS 3, CREAM CITY NINE 2, IN TEN

The shortstop of the Metropolitans compressed a season's worth of service into two innings. With the bases choked and two out in the ninth of a tied game, Francisco Lindor raced to his right and took Hamilton's soft liner off the turf with a full-length dive, saving the go-ahead runs; in the tenth he crossed with the winning tally when Morel's fielder's-choice bounder was compounded by Hamilton's answering throwing error. Lindor had earlier homered, his thirteenth, and Robert Jr. added his tenth; Yelich's ninth-inning double had briefly rescued Milwaukee. The Brewers, still owners of the game's best record at one-and-eighty wins, have nonetheless dropped two running in Flushing.

CLARK ATONES INSIDE THE SPAN OF AN INNING: DETROITS 4, RAYS 1

The young center fielder Max Clark botched a bad-hop liner in the fourth — the sort of carom that changes direction as if bribed — and was still cursing himself when he stepped in against the left-hander Seymour an inning later. His answer: a go-ahead two-run homer into the right-field seats, the second of his major-league life and his first at Comerica Park, struck with such absorbed attention that he carried his bat nearly to first base. Lee added a late insurance single, Jansen closed for his seventeenth save, and the Tampa men — beaten while the Americans were also losing — hold their lead in the East at three games and a half.

KIRBY FURIOUS, AND THE SOUND MEN KEEP CLIMBING: PUGET SOUND MEN 4, QUAKERS 1

George Kirby was all business by the Sound: seven and two-thirds innings, six hits, a single run, nine strikeouts, with Nola — seven strikeouts of his own — the hard-luck loser. Cal Raleigh, a mere evening removed from the three-homer performance this paper celebrated at length, homered again, his eighteenth, and Canzone's two-run single in the seventh furnished the cushion before Muñoz sealed his four-and-twentieth save. The Quakers have now lost two straight since their nine-game streak was buried, and Seattle has won two straight in the climb back toward the wild-card row.

GOODMAN'S FIVE-AND-THIRTIETH TRAVELS WELL, AND THE CAPITAL GOES HUNGRY: MOUNTAIN MEN 3, CAPITAL NINE 1

Hunter Goodman struck his five-and-thirtieth home run — third in the National's table, behind only Schwarber's nine-and-thirty and Olson's six-and-thirty — and Norby doubled home another in the same fourth inning. Lile answered at once with his seventeenth, but Washington found nothing further, and a fifth-inning Colorado run scored on a wild pitch stood as garnish. Romano closed for his thirteenth save; the Capital nine have now lost eight of their last ten, and the Mountain men, whatever their station in the standings, have avenged Monday's thirteen-to-three drubbing in the same yard.

AN IMMACULATE INNING WASTED, AND THE ELEPHANTS TAKE THE EVENING: ATHLETICS 4, TWINS 2

Carlos Cortes opened the scoring with a two-run homer in the second and Sacramento added two more in the sixth on White's double and Walton's single, which proved sufficient against a Minnesota attack held to four hits. The Twins' consolations were historic rather than arithmetical — Bradley's nine-pitch masterpiece in the fifth, for which see the annals desk — and their anxieties are medical, Buxton's hip having ended his evening early, for which see the infirmary ward. Jump took the win, Alvarado the save, his fourth.

CAVANAUGH EARLY, DEVERS LOUD, AND STEWART'S NINETY-NINTH ARRIVES TOO LATE: FRISCO NINE 3, REDLEGS 1

The Frisco nine did their scoring at the bookends of the evening's first half — Cavanaugh's two-run single in the opening frame and Devers's eight-and-twentieth homer in the fifth — and the pitching did the rest, Cincinnati held to four hits, the win to the young Molina and the save to Seymour. The Redleg run arrived in the ninth by way of Sal Stewart's homer, likewise his eight-and-twentieth, which carried him to nine-and-ninety runs batted in and the doorstep of the century, as the milestone desk relates. Cincinnati has dropped three straight; the Frisco men have quietly won two.

The arithmetic desk reports the American's furniture rearranged yet again. The West's crown, which sat upon two uneasy heads Monday morning and upon Texas alone on Tuesday, this morning passes to Houston by the half-game — the third head to wear it in as many editions. The final wild-card chair remains Cleveland's, its tenant at seven-and-sixty wins against six-and-sixty defeats and winner of six running, with Texas one game astern, Baltimore two and a half, and Seattle, Minnesota, and Toronto three. In the National the chairs read: the Cubs comfortable, Philadelphia at two games' cushion, and San Diego clinging to the last seat with Arizona now a single game behind and Miami four. Tonight the card again runs to the full fifteen engagements, all verified against the schedule: the rubber match in the desert goes at 3:40 by the Eastern clock, the Bucs seek a sweep of the Friars at 4:10, the Cleveland nine and the Anaheim nine resume at 4:07, the Houstons and the Americans take up the crown question again in the Bronx at 7:05, the Royals carry nine straight into Toronto at 7:07, and the champions and the Tomahawk nine stage the second act of their collision at 7:15. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE DESK'S APPOINTMENT IS KEPT, THOUGH NOT AS PHILADELPHIA DREW IT: RALEIGH, LONG BECALMED, STRIKES THREE HOME RUNS, WHEELER IS CHASED, AND THE STREAK DIES AT NINE — MARINERS 9, PHILADELPHIAS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 48 · Tuesday, the Five-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 10 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE DESK'S APPOINTMENT IS KEPT, THOUGH NOT AS PHILADELPHIA DREW IT: RALEIGH, LONG BECALMED, STRIKES THREE HOME RUNS, WHEELER IS CHASED, AND THE STREAK DIES AT NINE — MARINERS 9, PHILADELPHIAS 2

The catcher who began the evening batting .159 ends it the thirteenth man in Seattle's annals with a three-homer game — a two-run blast to crown a five-run first, a back-to-back salvo with Young to open the fifth, a solo shot in the seventh — while the Philadelphia nine, riders of a season-best winning streak this paper has chronicled at every length, are sent to bed with two runs and a battered ace

The reader will recall that yesterday's desk note directed all eyes to Seattle at 9:40 Eastern, where Wheeler and his ten victories were to oppose Gilbert, and the Philadelphia nine were to unpack a nine-game winning streak from their westward luggage. The appointment was kept to the minute; the script was burned in the first inning. Philadelphia scratched a run from Bohm's ground-out, whereupon the home nine answered with five — Julio Rodríguez clearing the fence with two aboard for his twentieth, and Cal Raleigh, the switch-hitting catcher whose season has been one long penance at .159, capping the frame with a two-run blast. It was the first sentence of the finest chapter of his life.

For Raleigh opened the fifth with another homer, Cole Young followed him over the wall on the very next argument — the back-to-back salvo that chased Wheeler from the premises — and in the seventh he struck a third, a solo shot off the reliever Shugart, all three driven to the right-field quarter. No man had ever seen him do it: "I had never done that before — at any level. So, hard to fathom, and it was a fun night," the author testified, having gone three-for-three with a walk and lifted his average from .159 to .167. The researchers certify him the thirteenth Mariner to strike three home runs in a game — the last being his clubmate Canzone only last September — and the only other Seattle catcher ever to do it is one Dan Wilson, who now writes the lineup card on which Raleigh's name appears. The manager's fraternity, one supposes, has its own ways of passing down a trade secret.

The wreckage on the other side was considerable: Wheeler, sovereign of ten victories against four defeats at the evening's start, was relieved of nine hits, eight runs, and four home runs inside four innings, and departs at ten-and-five; Realmuto's ninth homer was the visitors' lone late ornament. Logan Gilbert took the decision, his eleventh, on five workmanlike innings. Thus the finest streak of Philadelphia's season perishes at nine — the Philadelphias remain three and a half astern of Atlanta and keep the National's second wild-card chair, so the mourning need not be prolonged — while the Emerald City nine, who gave their faithful two walk-off deliverances Friday and Saturday and then absorbed Chicago's nineteen-run sermon Sunday, have now taken three of four in that yard and stand three games from the American's final chair. The Sound, it appears, declines to be dull.

News Around the League

THE FRONT-OFFICE DESK: HOUSTON AND ITS GENERAL MANAGER PART COMPANY IN THE THICK OF A PENNANT RACE, AND ESPADA RETURNS TO HIS POST

The Houston club and its general manager Dana Brown have parted ways, the club announcing Monday what the wires describe as a mutual conclusion to a tenure begun in January of 2023 — two division titles to its credit, a contract expiring with the season, and a club that has lost six of its last eight engagements. The portfolio passes in commission to the assistant general managers Cook, Dickey, and Huff and to the senior adviser Jeff Bagwell, with the owner Crane overseeing the baseball operations himself through the transition — an arrangement the Herald observes without endorsement, owners' oversight of baseball matters having a mixed record in the annals. The timing is remarkable: the Houstons wake this morning half a game astern of the Lone Star nine in the West, their crown mislaid in idleness. There is gentler news from the same clubhouse — the manager Joe Espada, called away by a family emergency, rejoins his men for this evening's opener in the Bronx, which the schedule confirms for five minutes past seven, Eastern.

THE LABOR QUESTION: MANFRED PLEDGES THAT BASEBALL MEANS TO PLAY IN '27, AND THE HERALD TAKES THE PLEDGE UNDER ADVISEMENT

From the same Williamsport broadcast that appointed next year's Little League Classic — as this paper related Monday — the Commissioner Manfred addressed the graver matter: the collective bargain between the clubs and the players' union expires at one minute before midnight on the first of December, and the question of the 2027 season hangs upon its renewal. "We want to make a deal. We want to play baseball next year. We're planning on playing baseball next year," the Commissioner declared, reporting weekly conferences between the parties. The Herald prints the pledge faithfully and notes what follows it: the owners' chief object in the negotiation is a salary cap, the union's answer that the economic order wants no such overhaul — their asks running instead to a raised minimum wage, a loosened luxury-tax collar, and a fattened bonus pool for the young and underpaid — and the wires' sober assessment that, failing a bargain by the deadline, the likeliest course is a lockout of the players by the owners, shutting the game's business entire. On the merits the Herald's sympathies are of record and lie with the workingmen; as for the owners' capacity to pay, the reader need only consult the counting-house item below, where a franchise has just changed hands for a sum with a b in it.

THE COUNTING-HOUSE DESK: SAN DIEGO'S NEW PROPRIETORS ARRIVE WITH A SONG, TWO JERSEYS, AND THREE THOUSAND NINE HUNDRED MILLIONS

The Padres formally presented their new proprietors Monday at Petco Park: Jose E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones, husband and wife, who purchased the franchise at a valuation of $3.9 billion — the grandest price ever fetched by a baseball club — and were approved without dissent by the other nine-and-twenty owners a week past. The hour-long introduction opened with a song of Ms. Jones' own composition and closed with the couple in customized jerseys, and between came the substance: the purchase styled a "family investment," a pledge to spend "ambitiously" yet "judiciously," and repeated homage to the late Peter Seidler, whose open-handed stewardship the faithful of San Diego remember warmly. "We wanna win," Mr. Feliciano summarized. The Herald extends its welcome, notes that forty thousand four hundred forty-seven attended that very evening's twelve-inning engagement — the card below has its sorrows — and files the sale price where it belongs: in the ledger consulted whenever an owner next pleads poverty.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: FAIRBANKS' ARM SOUNDS ITS ALARM AGAIN, TOGLIA AND EMERSON GO UNDER THE KNIFE, AND PHOENIX HOPES FOR MARTE WITHIN THE WEEK

The gravest entry issues from Miami, where the closer Pete Fairbanks — seven seasons a Ray, now the Marlins' keeper of eighteen saves — felt nerve irritation and numbness through his throwing arm in the ninth inning Monday, walked the only man he faced, and departed; the walk became the deciding run, as the card below relates. The complaint is an old acquaintance, having cost him three weeks after a like episode in April — "Both of them weren't good," the patient allowed — and he submits to examinations this day.

Two seasons end upon the operating table. In Cincinnati, Michael Toglia — whose wounded shoulder this paper's ward first recorded Saturday — has his torn labrum repaired Tuesday, the price of a diving catch made in Arizona; the manager Francona reports the man had sworn he could play, which is admirable and immaterial. And in Seattle, the rookie shortstop Colt Emerson, one-and-twenty years of age and owner of an eight-year fortune signed before he had played a major-league game, will have a wrist tendon set right Wednesday, his trying freshman season closed at .190; the club expects him whole by spring, and his clubmate Bryan Woo, pronounced fit, takes his scheduled turn Wednesday. In Phoenix, at last, a hopeful line: the Diamondbacks believe Ketel Marte — whose saga this paper has chronicled past all appetite — may rejoin the lineup within the week.

THE MILESTONE DESK: STEWART STANDS TWO SHORT OF A HUNDRED, THE CARDINAL PAIR LURK AT SIX-AND-NINETY, AND ALVAREZ'S CROWN OF THREE SURVIVES AN IDLE MONDAY

The freshman Sal Stewart of Cincinnati was held without a tally in Monday's whitewash by the Bay, and so stands where he stood: eight-and-ninety runs driven home, master of all baseball's table, two short of the hundred mark and still pursuing the distinction — unclaimed by any rookie since 1950 — of leading the major leagues outright. His shadow has two heads and wears Cardinal red: Burleson and Walker, six-and-ninety apiece, idle Monday and losing no ground. In the American the arithmetic likewise kept the Sabbath: Yordan Alvarez, his club unengaged, holds his crown of three untouched — .320, six-and-thirty homers, ninety runs driven in, first in every column — though the Herald notes Caminero of Tampa Bay one homer astern, and observes that a Triple Crown defended from a deck chair is defended all the same.

The Rest of the Card

TWO IN THE NINTH, TAKEN FROM A WOUNDED HAND: RED SOX 4, MIAMI NINE 2, AND THE COUNT RUNS TO FOUR STRAIGHT

For eight innings Miami had the better of the argument's texture — Alcantara dealing seven innings of one-run ball — and none of its arithmetic: Abreu scored the equalizer on a wild pitch in the eighth, and in the ninth the stricken Fairbanks walked Gasper and departed with the arm trouble the infirmary ward records, whereupon Seigler tripled home the go-ahead run and Sogard singled in another. Chapman barred the door for his thirtieth save. Four straight now for the New Englanders, seven of ten, their wild-card cushion ample; the walk Fairbanks issued became his defeat, and the Miami nine slip to four astern of the National's final chair.

THE MACHINE DOES NOT REQUIRE DRAMA: GULF COAST CLUB 4, TIGERS 1, AND RASMUSSEN MAKES IT SEVEN RUNNING

Drew Rasmussen collected his seventh consecutive victory by the simplest of recipes — six innings, three hits, one run — while Aranda supplied a sixteenth homer and two runs driven in, Simpson dropped a bunt for a run with the insolence of a man batting .312, and Baker sealed his eight-and-thirtieth save. The league leaders thus hold their three-and-a-half-game advantage over the Bronx; the Tigers, whose evening amounted to five hits and Callahan's sacrifice fly, have now dropped six running — one victory in their last ten — and the Motor City's September reading grows grim.

THE SHORTSTOP RETURNS AND THE OFFENSE REMEMBERS ITSELF: POTOMAC NINE 13, MILE HIGH NINE 3

Restored to the lineup, CJ Abrams scored twice, stole twice, and presided over a thirteen-run festival — Daylen Lile the chief celebrant with three hits, a sixteenth homer, and five runs driven in, Vivas adding three hits of his own — while Cade Cavalli struck out seven across six innings for his twelfth victory. "Now we go," runs the clubhouse verdict on the wires. For Colorado, Tovar's two hits and a homer were the ornament on a seventh consecutive defeat; the Mile High nine departed the Capital outscored beyond argument.

SEAGER CONDUCTS, BURGER AND LANGFORD SUPPLY THE BRASS, AND THE WEST'S CROWN FINDS A SINGLE HEAD: LONE STAR NINE 11, CHICAGOS 2

Texas struck early, often, and then again: Seager three hits and three runs driven in with a pair of doubles, Burger a two-and-twentieth homer among his two hits, Langford a fifteenth to close the accounts, fourteen hits in the whole demonstration behind Rocker's eight strikeouts. The visiting defense contributed its own theater — Nimmo at full extension above the right-field fence to rob Benintendi outright — and the home dugout its melancholy: Pederson, denied upon a challenge to the automated ball-strike arbiter, banged his bat and was invited to leave. Peters' two-run homer, the tenth of his year, was all the Chicagos could answer; and with Houston idle, the Lone Star nine take sole possession of the West's chair at six-and-sixty wins against the like number of defeats — a crown at the break-even line, but a crown unshared.

A HOMER FOR THE VISITING PEWS: GUARDIANS 4, SERAPHS 2, AND THE STREAK REACHES FIVE

Austin Hedges, with his parents in attendance, struck a two-run homer — his fifth — that stood as the difference, Kwan collected two hits, and Messick pitched to his tenth victory before Smith closed his four-and-thirtieth save. A fifth consecutive victory for Cleveland, seven of ten by the ledger, and the consequence is recorded in this evening's desk note: the American's final wild-card chair, so long a boarding-house, now holds a single tenant. The Seraphs' consolations were two hits off the bench from Lowe and the certainty of a warm evening in Anaheim.

GAUSMAN DEALS SEVEN SPOTLESS AND THE DESERT GOES HUNGRY: CUBS 7, DIAMONDBACKS 0

Kevin Gausman threw seven scoreless innings on three hits, and his employers, fresh from Sunday's nineteen-run sermon by the Sound, kept the pulpit: Conforto three hits with a twelfth homer, Carson Kelly an eighth, the rookie Pedro Ramírez a triple among his two hits, and a three-run sixth followed by two more in the seventh to end the suspense. The whitewash is Chicago's second consecutive victory; for Arizona it is a graver matter, the Diamondbacks falling two games astern of San Diego in the pursuit of the National's final chair — with, as the infirmary ward relates, hope of Marte's return the week's best medicine.

BUXTON SCORES FROM EVERYWHERE AND THE NINTH-INNING RALLY ARRIVES TOO LATE: NORTH STARS 9, WHITE ELEPHANTS 6

Buxton crossed the plate four times upon three hits, the rookie Culpepper collected four hits, Bell drove home three, and Zebby Matthews carried a commanding evening through seven innings; when the White Elephants awoke for four runs in the ninth — McNeil, Gelof, and Butler doubling in file — the awakening was academic, and Morris recorded the final out for the save. Sixteen hits for the North Stars, who remain two from the American's final chair; for the Athletics, a twelve-hit evening wasted, and a reminder that arithmetic performed in the ninth earns no interest.

TWELVE INNINGS, FOUR HOURS AND TEN MINUTES, AND ONE RUN TO SHOW THE NEW PROPRIETORS: CORSAIRS 3, PADRES 2

On the very evening San Diego's new owners took their bows — the counting-house desk has the ceremony — forty thousand four hundred forty-seven watched the home nine spend twelve innings discovering that the visitors would not oblige. Valdez's fifteenth homer and Flores Jr.'s double built Pittsburgh's lead; a balk and Cronenworth's eighth-inning single leveled it; and in the twelfth Nick Gonzales — he of the .308 average, second in the National's batting table — singled home Triolo for the verdict. Yates profited, Ramírez sealed his second save, and the Padres' grip on the National's third chair holds at two games over Arizona, the evening's four hours and ten minutes notwithstanding.

FIVE RUNS IN TWO INNINGS OFF THE FOURTEEN-GAME WINNER, AND THE SHORN GIANTS SHUT OUT THE REDS: JINTS 5, CINCINNATI 0

The San Franciscans took the field Monday having consigned four men to the infirmary in a single day's transactions — Adames' elbow, Bericoto's knee, Brubaker's ribs, and Eldridge away on bereavement — recalled five from Sacramento to fill the pews, and then played their finest game in a fortnight: five runs inside two innings off Chase Burns, owner of fourteen victories against but two defeats at the evening's start, crowned by Devers' three-run homer, his seven-and-twentieth. Six pitchers passed the whitewash hand to hand, Foley taking the decision. Burns falls to fourteen-and-three; the Reds, blanked on five hits and further bereaved of Toglia — see the ward — find their September arithmetic unimproved.

The arithmetic desk reports a morning of consequence at both ends of the American's ledger. The final wild-card chair, which has been let by the room and by the half-week all month, this morning holds one tenant alone: Cleveland, winners of five running, at six-and-sixty wins against six-and-sixty defeats — and thus, for the first time in this desk's recent chronicle, the chair's occupant sits no lower than the break-even line. The eviction was accomplished upward, Texas departing the wild-card row entirely to take sole possession of the West's crown at the identical break-even figure, with Houston half a game astern in both accountings and this morning without a general manager besides, as the front-office desk relates. Behind Cleveland: Houston at half a game, Minnesota and Toronto two, Baltimore two and a half, Seattle three. In the National the chairs hold — the Cubs, Philadelphia with its streak freshly buried at nine, and San Diego, with Arizona two astern and Miami four. The card this evening runs to the full fifteen engagements, all verified against the schedule: the Brewers send Harrison and his ten victories to Flushing at 7:10; the champions and the Atlantas resume their collision at 7:15, Glasnow opposing Elder; Espada resumes his post as the Houstons open in the Bronx at 7:05; and by the Pacific, Skenes and his hundred-and-seventy-one strikeouts visit San Diego at 9:40. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
