entry.title: THREE LETTERS FILL THE WRIGLEY NIGHT, AND THE TENTH INNING ANSWERS THEM: CROW-ARMSTRONG OPENS THE GAME WITH A HOMER, ENDS IT WITH ANOTHER, AND SEALS A SECOND STRAIGHT THIRTY-AND-THIRTY — CUBS 7, WHITE SOX 5
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 41 · Tuesday, the Eighteenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 11 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THREE LETTERS FILL THE WRIGLEY NIGHT, AND THE TENTH INNING ANSWERS THEM: CROW-ARMSTRONG OPENS THE GAME WITH A HOMER, ENDS IT WITH ANOTHER, AND SEALS A SECOND STRAIGHT THIRTY-AND-THIRTY — CUBS 7, WHITE SOX 5

The crosstown engagement this paper billed last evening delivers everything promised and history besides — the center fielder leads off the first with his nine-and-twentieth homer, watches the South Siders seize the lead twice, and with a man aboard in the tenth dispatches his thirtieth over the right-field wall to win it outright, becoming the first Cub ever to post consecutive seasons of thirty homers and thirty stolen bases, and but the sixth man in all the game's annals to begin a game with a home run and end it with one

The chant rose out of the Wrigley Field night before the tenth inning was fairly begun — three letters, over and over, forty thousand voices strong — for the faithful had done the arithmetic and knew who was due. Pete Crow-Armstrong had opened the evening's account in the first inning with a leadoff thunderbolt to right, his nine-and-twentieth of the season; now, with Carson Kelly aboard and the crosstown affair knotted at five, he answered his own overture. The two-run blow that cleared the right-field wall was his thirtieth homer of the campaign, and as it carried he wheeled toward his own dugout and flung the bat with a violence the occasion excused entirely. 'I usually black out during those type of things,' the young man confessed afterward. 'I got a good bat flip in — I know that.'

Let the record state what the moment contained. With thirty home runs beside one-and-thirty stolen bases, Crow-Armstrong becomes the first Cub in the franchise's long history to fashion thirty-and-thirty seasons in consecutive years, and but the tenth man ever to do it, joining a register that runs from Willie Mays through Bonds father and son to Witt and Ramírez of the present age; he and Sammy Sosa remain the only Cubs to have done it even once. The Elias scribes add a garland: only five men before him — Vic Power the first, in 1957 — had ever struck a leadoff homer and a walk-off homer in the same game. 'It's been incredible to watch,' said the manager Craig Counsell, and his starter Shota Imanaga, who fanned ten South Siders across six innings in his own right, went further: 'You watch him play, and make the fantastic plays that he does, and you're not really surprised... he always passes it.'

The game deserved its finish. Seiya Suzuki had followed Crow-Armstrong's opening blast with one of his own, back-to-back before an out was recorded, whereupon the visitors clawed to the front on Randal Grichuk's three-run homer in the fourth — the lone blemish upon Imanaga's evening — and, after Nico Hoerner's two-run single (abetted by a Vargas throwing error) had restored the Cubs' advantage, Andrew Benintendi stunned the premises with a two-run go-ahead blow in the eighth. Hoerner, four hits on the night, singled home the leveler in the ninth; Jacob Webb escaped a bases-filled tenth without a scratch; and the stage was thus swept clean for the finale. The ledger takes its own notes: Chicago's North Side club stands at three-and-seventy wins against three-and-fifty defeats, holder of the National's first wild-card chair by six full games and four and a half behind the idle Milwaukees, while the Pale Hose — still masters of the American's Central by four and a half — were reminded that the rivalry keeps no standings. The two clubs reconvene at Wrigley this very evening.

News Around the League

THE CASE OF THE ABSENT SECOND BASEMAN: MARTE FAILS TO APPEAR AT FENWAY, AND ARIZONA INVOKES THE RESTRICTED LIST

The strangest wire of the morning issues from Boston, where the Diamondbacks took the field without Ketel Marte — not injured, not suspended, but simply absent. The second baseman did not appear at Fenway Park for the series opener, owing to what the club would later term a 'personal matter,' and was placed upon the restricted list. The manager Torey Lovullo allowed that he first caught wind of the possibility upon waking Monday morning, and declined to detail his communications with the man. The Herald notes that Marte's knee had already cost him time this month, as this paper's infirmary column has chronicled; what has cost him now is a mystery the club is in no hurry to solve publicly. The Arizonas could ill afford the distraction on the evening's evidence — the particulars of their eleven-to-one undoing are rendered upon the card below — and their grip on the wild-card scramble loosens by the day.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: FRIED'S ELBOW SENDS HIM BACK, RODÓN STEPS INTO THE BREACH, AND SWANSON'S SENTENCE IS MADE OFFICIAL

The Bronx ward reports a revolving door. Max Fried has been returned to the fifteen-day injured list with a bone bruise in his left elbow, the move backdated to Friday — the same joint, be it noted, that cost him better than two months earlier this season, hyperextended rather than struck. The counterweight arrived within the hour: Carlos Rodón, shelved since the third of July with inflammation of his own left elbow, is activated to take the ball this very evening at Baltimore, stepping into the rotation turn Fried vacates. In Chicago, the verdict this paper's ward forecast on Sunday is now official: Dansby Swanson goes to the ten-day list with a strain of the left oblique, having felt his side seize upon a single swing — 'It just felt like my left side kind of tightened up on me,' said the shortstop — a hard subtraction from a Cubs infield in full stretch-run stride. And from Denver, a brighter entry: Shohei Ohtani, whose evening's carpentry is described below, may ascend a bullpen mound as soon as this day, the wires report, in the next step of his long march back to pitching.

COMMERCE AT THE HIGHEST TABLE: THE PADRES PASS TO NEW HANDS BY UNANIMOUS CONSENT

The owners of all thirty clubs have spoken with one voice: the transfer of the San Diego franchise to the group led by Kwanza Jones and José E. Feliciano has been unanimously approved, the league announced Monday, essentially completing a sale the Seidler family agreed to in May. Jones and Feliciano will jointly lead the ownership, with Feliciano designated the club's control person. The ballplayers marked the occasion in their own fashion, dropping a one-run decision at Flushing hours later — the new proprietors will learn soon enough that the franchise plays its closest games at the least convenient hours.

THE AWARDS DESK TAKES ITS STRAW POLL: SCHLITTLER AND MISIOROWSKI ALL BUT MEASURED FOR THEIR HARDWARE

The wire's latest canvass of five-and-thirty experts on the Cy Young question returns a verdict scarcely worth the suspense: Jacob Misiorowski of Milwaukee was the unanimous choice of every voter in the National, and Cam Schlittler of the Yankees claimed five-and-twenty of the five-and-thirty first-place ballots in the American. The ledger offers no rebuttal. Misiorowski proprietors a 1.75 earned-run figure and two hundred ten strikeouts, both the National's finest by comfortable margins; Schlittler's 2.19 leads the American, with his hundred eighty-nine strikeouts third besides. Six weeks remain for an upset, and the desk, having consulted the arithmetic, declines to predict one.

THE ALMANAC DESK: WILLIAMSPORT ON SUNDAY, AND SIX WEEKS TO THE WIRE

Two entries for the long calendar. First: the Little League Classic arrives Sunday next, the three-and-twentieth of August, when the Brewers and Braves repair to Williamsport to perform before the smallest and sternest jury in baseball — a fixture this paper has commended before and commends again. Second, the hourglass: the almanac fixes the final day of the regular season at the seven-and-twentieth of September, some six weeks distant — which, given the condition of the wild-card furniture described in the desk note below, is either far too long or nowhere near long enough, depending upon the reader's rooting interest.

The Rest of the Card

THE SWEEP IS FORBIDDEN, AS COMMISSIONED: RAYS 7, ORIOLES 6, WITH BAKER TAKING FIVE OUTS FOR HIS FIVE-AND-THIRTIETH

The commission this paper recorded yesterday — Shane McClanahan, activated expressly to prevent a four-game Baltimore sweep at the Trop — was duly executed, though hardly in the manner drawn up. The returning left-hander gave three and a third innings in his first appearance from the injured list, struck out three, and surrendered a four-hundred-sixty-eight-foot moonshot to Coby Mayo, whose evening also included a double and two runs batted in. The O's built a six-to-four lead upon the long ball — Alonso's eight-and-twentieth, Encarnacion-Strand's two-run blow atop a two-run single, four driven in for the young man in all — but the seventh undid them: Aranda singled home one and DeLuca two more, and then Bryan Baker, fresh and unbothered, recorded the final five outs without incident, the first save of such length in his career and his five-and-thirtieth of the season, the largest crop in the game. The Tampa Bay nine, at five-and-seventy wins, remain the American's class; Baltimore's punishment for the defeat is rendered in the desk note's arithmetic.

FIFTEEN STRIKEOUTS AND TWO EARLY RUNS CARRY THE OPENER: CARDS 2, CINCINNATIS 1

The first game of the Cincinnati doubleheader was settled in its opening minutes and defended for two hours thereafter. Alec Burleson lined a two-run double in the first — his two-and-ninetieth runs batted in keep him atop the National's table — and the St. Louis pitching corps spent the rest of the afternoon fanning Redlegs at a prodigious rate: fifteen strikeouts in all, the home nine held to three hits, with Gastelum taking the decision in relief and O'Brien closing for his one-and-thirtieth save, the National's largest count. The lone Cincinnati answer was Dane Myers' fourth homer; the reader is advised to remember the name for approximately one entry.

MYERS TIES IT IN THE NINTH, AND ELLY ENDS IT IN THE TENTH — HIS FIRST WALK-OFF EVER: CINCINNATIS 6, CARDS 5

The nightcap repaid the afternoon with interest. Consigned to the designated hitter's post after an oh-for-four with four strikeouts in the opener — 'I think he knew he was going to lose that one anyway,' deadpanned the manager Terry Francona of the negotiation — Elly De La Cruz found himself at the plate in the tenth with Stephenson aboard and the game level, and laced a double to left that ended it: the first walk-off of the two-time All-Star's career. The road to that moment wound considerably: St. Louis led five-to-four in the ninth behind Herrera's fourteenth homer and Torres' go-ahead single, whereupon the aforementioned Dane Myers — he of the opener's only run — cleared the wall a second time in a single day to force the extra frame. Pagán took the decision; the clubs split the twin bill and remain locked together in the wild-card table's outer orbit, three games from the last chair.

SÁNCHEZ COLLECTS HIS SIXTEENTH, AND A REPLAY GLASS TAKES A RUN OFF MIAMI'S TABLE: PHILADELPHIAS 6, MIAMI NINE 5

Cristopher Sánchez — six-and-ten victories now against four defeats, the National's largest total — ground through six innings of one-run ball at home, and Philadelphia needed nearly every crumb of the lead its small-ball assembled: run-scoring singles by Turner, Arraez, and Bohm, a Schwarber sacrifice fly, and two driven in by Hill, the second upon a bases-loaded walk. The seventh inning supplied the controversy. Down three with the sacks full, Sanoja laced a ball down the first-base line, called foul upon the field; the replay glass ruled it fair, but the magistrates awarded only two runs, returning Lopez to third — a bases-clearing double by any natural reading — whereupon the Miami manager Clayton McCullough delivered his opinion of the proceedings and was invited to leave. Navarreto's first homer of the year and Lopez's ninth-inning single brought the Fish within one before Duran barred the door, his seven-and-twentieth save. The Phils have won four running and hold the National's second chair by a game; Miami departs three back, muttering about geometry.

McGONIGLE THUNDERS, SOMMERS SPRINTS, AND THE DETROITS REJOIN THE CHAIR FIGHT: TIGERS 8, ALLEGHENYS 5

Detroit built its evening at Pittsburgh early and generously: two in the first upon singles by McKinstry and Lee, Kevin McGonigle's two-run homer — his thirteenth — in the second, and a three-run sixth capped by Callahan's two-run single, fourteen hits in the visitors' ledger by night's end. The Alleghenys made their argument in their own sixth, Yorke's bases-clearing double the loudest word of a four-run reply, before Valdez handed matters to the relief corps and Jansen closed for his sixteenth save. The evening's curiosity belonged to the young reliever Drew Sommers, who broke off the mound on a chopper to Torkelson's right and won the footrace to the bag by a stride over Mangum and his elite wheels — 'Thankfully I was just a little bit faster than him,' the pitcher reported. The victory lifts Detroit level with Baltimore and Texas for the American's final chair, of which more below.

SIXTEEN HITS, AND THE ABANDONED ARIZONAS ARE BURIED: HUB NINE 11, DIAMONDBACKS 1

Whatever disorder attended Arizona's morning — see the news columns for the Marte affair — the evening offered no refuge. Boston battered the visitors with sixteen hits, Ceddanne Rafaela alone contributing three doubles to run his season's count to two-and-thirty, Sogard adding two more two-baggers, Contreras his five-and-twentieth homer, and Gasper his first of the year with two driven in. The pitching was arranged in the club's newest fashion: an opener to begin, then Brayan Bello in the bulk role he has lately made an argument in, four and two-thirds innings of one-run ball for the victory — fifty strikes among his six-and-seventy pitches. The Hub nine thus shake off a two-and-seven stumble in emphatic style; Arizona, held to four hits, has dropped two running and slips a game behind San Diego in the chair scramble.

TWICE THEY TESTED THE YOUNG MAN'S ARM, AND TWICE THEY DIED AT THE PLATE: METS 2, SAN DIEGO NINE 1

The whole of this taut affair at Flushing was contained in its first inning. New York scored twice — Bichette singling home one, Robert Jr. lofting home the other — and San Diego promptly ran itself out of the reply. With runners at first and second, France singled to right, whereupon Cronenworth was dispatched home and thrown out by Carson Benge, the ball arriving at very nearly a hundred miles per hour. One batter later Merrill singled to the same address, the third-base coach waved Machado around, and Benge threw him out as well — a hundred and three and nine-tenths miles per hour this time, the first Met ever to cut down two runners at the plate in a single inning. Thus armored, Nolan McLean worked six innings of one-run ball for his ninth victory, Buehler was hard-luck opposite with two hits allowed across six, and Duarte closed. The Metropolitans have won four running; the Friars, whose new owners are toasted in the news columns, were welcomed to the family with a lesson in outfield ballistics.

WITT DRIVES IN THREE AND THE MISSOURIANS MAKE IT TWO RUNNING: ROYALS 9, ATHLETICS 5

Kansas City spotted Jeff McNeil a leadoff homer and then buried the gesture beneath thirteen hits: three in the first upon Garcia's single and Perez's two-run knock, Bobby Witt Jr.'s two-run homer — his fifteenth — in the second, and steady contributions thereafter, Witt finishing with three driven in, a double, and his three-and-thirtieth stolen base, with Caglianone singling home a pair for good measure. The Athletics kept a respectable countenance through White's and Serven's middle-inning homers — three round-trippers in all for the visitors — but Wacha weathered the lot across five innings for the decision and Cruz closed. The Kansas City nine, whatever their station in the ledger, have won two straight; the wandering Athletics have not been so fortunate, and the clubs go again this evening.

FOUR IN THE FIRST FROM THE NEW LEADOFF MAN'S SPARK: MINNESOTANS 4, BRAVES 2

Luke Keaschall, handed the leadoff post for the first time all season, opened the home first with a double and set a four-run rally going before the Atlanta starter had found his footing: Josh Bell's ground-rule double cashed two, Lewis and Clemens singled home the others, and that, remarkably, was the evening's entire Minnesota offense — and enough. The Braves' reply was confined to Acuña Jr.'s two-run single in the fifth, whereupon the Twins' relief corps pitched four and two-thirds scoreless innings to seal it, Adams taking the decision and Gómez his eighteenth save. 'It was good to get the bats going in the first,' offered Keaschall, a man unlikely to be evicted from his new post soon. The Dixie nine, still masters of the National's East by a comfortable margin, have dropped two of three; Minnesota lurks half a game from the American's final chair.

EIGHT HUNDRED SEVENTY-EIGHT FEET OF OHTANI, AND ONE SOUVENIR FOR THE BULLPEN: TROLLEY DODGERS 11, COLORADANS 5

The thin air of Denver received the full Shohei treatment. Ohtani collected four hits — the eleventh four-hit evening of his career — and cleared the fences twice, a leadoff blast in the fifth and a two-run drive in the sixth totaling eight hundred seventy-eight feet of flight, the second of them a four-hundred-fifty-two-foot artifact that landed in the glove of the Dodger reliever Kyle Hurt, stationed in the bullpen and clearly delighted with his keepsake. Muncy's three-run homer, his five-and-twentieth, had opened the breach in the third; Betts drove in two, Pages likewise; and Blake Snell, in the quietest headline of the night, delivered six innings of two-hit, one-run ball for his first victory of the season. The defeat fell to Sugano, roughed for seven runs across five innings, his ledger falling to twelve-and-six. Los Angeles, at five-and-seventy wins, stands two and a half behind Milwaukee for the game's best ledger; the Coloradans' evening is best measured in the souvenirs.

The arithmetic desk reports that the furniture has been rearranged again: the American's final wild-card chair, in Baltimore's sole keeping but four-and-twenty hours ago, is this morning shared by three tenants — the Orioles, the Rangers, and the Tigers, each at one-and-sixty wins against four-and-sixty defeats — with the Twins and Blue Jays half a game astern, Cleveland a full game, and Seattle two: seven claimants, and still not one of them at the break-even line. In the National the seating is more orderly: the Cubs hold the first chair by six, Philadelphia the second by a single game over San Diego, with Arizona one behind the Friars and Miami and St. Louis three back. This day's card runs to the full fifteen engagements. The bill of fare: at Baltimore at 6:35, Rodón makes his return from the injured list for the Yankees, opposite Baz; at Philadelphia at 6:40, Wheeler and his 2.89 receive the Miami nine; at the Trop at 6:40, Martinez — twelve victories against three, a 2.74 figure — takes the ball for Tampa Bay against Toronto; and at 8:05 the crosstown engagement resumes at Wrigley, Gausman handed the ball for the Cubs and the South Siders under every obligation to answer for the tenth inning. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE ACE THEY WOULD NOT SELL OUTDUELS THE ACE THEY COULD NOT BUY: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 2, AND THE BEST LEDGER IN BASEBALL RESIDES IN MILWAUKEE
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 40 · Monday, the Seventeenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE ACE THEY WOULD NOT SELL OUTDUELS THE ACE THEY COULD NOT BUY: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 2, AND THE BEST LEDGER IN BASEBALL RESIDES IN MILWAUKEE

Young Logan Henderson, the very arm Milwaukee refused to surrender in its deadline pursuit of Tarik Skubal, faces the great left-hander at Chavez Ravine and betters him across a career-longest seven innings — Bauers raps four hits, the series falls to the visitors three games to one, the season's set is claimed four to three, and the Cream City nine depart the coast with the finest record in all the game

Commerce, the wise men say, is settled at the deadline; Sunday in Los Angeles it was settled on the mound. A fortnight ago the Brewers tried mightily to purchase Tarik Skubal from the Dodgers and would not, it is reported, part with a twenty-four-year-old Texan named Logan Henderson to do it. Sunday the ledger explained itself. Henderson worked seven innings — the longest afternoon of his major-league life, and the first time he had cleared a seventh since his community-college days in Waco — permitting three hits and a single run, that upon Max Muncy's four-and-twentieth homer, walking one and striking out six. Skubal, for his part, was game but outdone: seven hits and two runs across six, one of the pair unearned, and a record now standing at seven-and-seven against Henderson's seven-and-two.

The Milwaukee offense was a study in patience rewarded. An unearned run in the second, gift of the first of Tommy Edman's two errors; Jake Bauers' run-scoring single in the fifth to restore the lead; then the professional's finish — Bauers doubling home Chourio in the seventh, Vaughn singling home Bauers behind him, and two more crossing in the ninth upon Edman's second miscue. Bauers finished with four hits, tying the best day of his career, and closed the series at six-for-thirteen with five walks besides — this the same man who, after the club was swept at San Diego to open the trip, counseled his mates toward calm in language the Herald shall gently paraphrase. 'Whatever happens in October is whatever happens,' he said Sunday, permitting himself a glance ahead, 'but I think the anticipation is we're going to have to get through these guys. We can play with them, and if we execute, we can beat them.' Chourio added three hits and three runs; Andy Pages' one-and-twentieth homer in the ninth supplied the Los Angeles postscript.

The consequences are considerable. Milwaukee takes the series, three games to one, in a rematch of last autumn's one-sided championship series; takes the season's set from Los Angeles, four games to three; and emerges from a gauntlet of seventeen games in seventeen days — ten of them won — at seven-and-seventy wins against eight-and-forty defeats, the best mark in the majors, three full games clear of the Dodgers, five clear of the Cubs in the Central, and two and a half clear of the field entire. 'It was really important to finish the 17-game stretch with a series win,' said Henderson, master of understatement. This day the Brewers rest, and no club in baseball has earned it more honestly.

News Around the League

THE HERALD LOWERS ITS COLORS: TOMMY JOHN, 1943–2026

The saddest wire of the morning comes draped in black: Tommy John, the durable left-hander whose two hundred and eighty-eight victories spanned six-and-twenty seasons and whose name passed from the roster into the anatomy textbook, has died at three-and-eighty years of age. He broke in with Cleveland in 1963 and threw his last pitch for the Yankees in 1989 at six-and-forty; between those bookends came four All-Star selections, consecutive twenty-win campaigns in the Bronx, and the second-most victories of any Modern Era pitcher not enshrined at Cooperstown. But it was a single pitch in July of 1974 — a fastball that ended with what he called a 'crash' in his left elbow — that made him immortal. When Dr. Frank Jobe proposed a never-attempted repair, borrowing a tendon from the pitcher's right forearm, he quoted odds of one in a hundred. 'You're a great doctor and I believe in you. But you're wrong. I will come back,' John told him — and did, missing 1975 entire, then winning twenty games in 1977 and finishing second in the Cy Young balloting, whereupon the writers took to calling him the Bionic Man. The procedure that bears his name has since returned careers beyond counting. 'Just how much of a trailblazer he was,' offered Gerrit Cole, himself among the repaired, '... really writing the script for how to push through it and overcome it.' The Dodgers' Stan Kasten judged that his courage 'can't be overstated'; the Yankee manager Aaron Boone remembered 'one of my favorite windups to imitate.' The Herald dips its masthead to a man who lent the game not merely his left arm but a second chance for every arm that came after — few players have given more to men they never met.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: SWANSON'S SIDE, McCLANAHAN'S RETURN, AND A BRONX WARD IN CONVALESCENCE

The freshest entry is Chicago's: Dansby Swanson departed the North Siders' Sunday defeat with discomfort in his left side, and though the machines will render their verdict, the club already expects a stay upon the injured list — poor tidings for a team that has now dropped two straight. Better news from the Gulf: Shane McClanahan, his back tightness resolved, returns to the Tampa Bay rotation this very night against Baltimore, with sweep-prevention his explicit commission. The Bronx ward reports progress by degrees: Cody Bellinger begins a rehabilitation assignment Tuesday and could return shortly thereafter; Aaron Judge, mending his fractured rib, has progressed to playing catch but not yet to swinging; Carlos Rodón takes an assignment Tuesday, venue undecided. Elsewhere in the ledger: Philadelphia's Trea Turner, who fouled a ball off his knee Saturday, required no imaging and sat Sunday only as a precaution; Washington handles James Wood and his tender oblique with kid gloves; the Dodgers have lodged Justin Wrobleski on the fifteen-day list with forearm inflammation; and Boston has made official the hamstring sentence of Masataka Yoshida, ten days at the least.

FORTY INNINGS, THIRTEEN MILLIONS: CHAPMAN'S OPTION VESTS, AND FOUR HUNDRED SAVES DRAW NEAR

When Aroldis Chapman closed out Saturday's whitewash at Pittsburgh, the ninth inning he recorded was worth rather more than the save it wasn't: it carried him past forty innings for the season, and with them the vesting option in his Boston contract. Let the ledger show: pass the year-end physical, and the flame-throwing left-hander — now eight-and-thirty years of age — wears Boston colors in 2027 at thirteen million dollars. He has earned every cent the old-fashioned way, a 1.17 earned-run figure last season and 1.99 this, with seven-and-twenty saves that tie him for sixth in the game and bring his career count to three hundred ninety-four — ninth upon the all-time table, six shy of the four-hundred summit. 'I feel like home here,' said the man whose fastball once made hitters feel anything but.

THE SHOES MAKE THE MAN, AND NOW COOPERSTOWN WANTS THE SHOES

A charming coda to Saturday's thunder at Wrigley: the Hall of Fame has requested the cleats in which Joshua Báez struck three home runs in his first three major-league at-bats — and the cleats were never his. The rookie arrived for his debut with a dirty pair and white batting gloves, whereupon the veteran Bryan Torres staged an intervention — 'You can't go out like that during your debut. You have to look sharp. You have to wear red' — and requisitioned a clean size-twelve pair from Blaze Jordan's locker, a red belt from a trainer, and batting gloves from José Fermín. Jordan, informed after the fact that history was being made in his footwear, gave the only possible answer: 'OK, 100 percent.' The borrowed shoes now travel to Cooperstown, where the game's first three-homer debut will be commemorated in leather that fit the moment better than it fit the occasion's haste. Of the young man's Sunday encore, see the St. Louis dispatch below — the fates, having spent themselves Saturday, took the day off.

THE ALMANAC DESK: A SABATHIA CLEARS HIS FIRST FENCE, WILLIAMSPORT AWAITS, AND TWO FOR ONE IN CINCINNATI

Three entries. First, the bloodlines: Carsten Sabathia III, twentieth-round selection of the Brewers this summer, struck the first home run of his professional life for Single-A Wilson on Sunday — a three-for-four afternoon that has him nine-for-twenty as a professional — while his father, the Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, threw his arms skyward in the family suite. Second, the calendar: the almanac fixes the Little League Classic for Sunday next, the twenty-third of August, when the Brewers and Braves repair to Williamsport to play before the smallest and most discerning audience in baseball. Third, this day's arithmetic: the Cardinals and Reds play two at Cincinnati — first pitch at 1:40, the nightcap at 6:40 — a full afternoon and evening of baseball for the price of a single admission to the wild-card scramble.

The Rest of the Card

SEVEN WITH TWO OUT IN THE SIXTH, AND THE BIRDS SEIZE THE WILD-CARD CHAIR OUTRIGHT: ORIOLES 10, TAMPA MEN 2

Read it twice if you must: Baltimore, at one-and-sixty wins against three-and-sixty defeats, this morning holds sole possession of the American's final wild-card seat. The Birds thrashed the league's best club a third consecutive time, and did it with the season's biggest inning — seven runs in the sixth, every one of them after two were out, Cowser's two-run homer, Holliday's two-run double, and Encarnacion-Strand's three-run double the heavy blows. Holliday finished with two hits and three runs batted in; Alonso doubled home two for his eightieth run driven in; Rogers gave six sturdy innings. 'We go out there and beat a good team three nights in a row, I don't think it's much of a fluke,' said Holliday, and the schedule invites him to prove it: the four-game sweep is on offer this very evening, with McClanahan activated expressly to forbid it. Tampa Bay, nine straight wins ago the hottest club in the game, has now dropped three running; Vilade's three hits and a homer were the lonely resistance.

THE REDBIRDS ROMP BEFORE THE NATION, ENCORE OR NO: CARDINALS 11, NORTH SIDERS 4

The nation tuned in for young Báez and stayed for everything else. The rookie went hitless in five with the whole country watching — the fates keep their own schedule — but his elders made the afternoon a rout: Burleson went three-for-five with a four-hundred-and-twenty-one-foot homer, his one-and-twentieth to tie the best of his career, four runs batted in raising his season's count to ninety; Walker matched him blow for blow with his four-and-twentieth homer, two doubles, and four runs driven in; and Wetherholt opened the game with a bloop double and came round three times. A six-run fourth broke it open, Dobbins struck out seven across five for the victory, and St. Louis claimed both the series and the season's set from Chicago, seven games to six. 'I know what August can do to you. I know what September can do for you,' said Burleson. The Redbirds, at three-and-sixty wins, sit three and a half from the National's last chair; the Cubs have dropped two straight and now welcome their South Side neighbors for three.

THE SINNER REDEEMED IN THE TENTH: BRONX BOMBERS 4, MAPLE LEAF NINE 3

Baseball's oldest morality play ran Sunday in Toronto. Ben Rice, promoted to the leadoff post in a general shuffling of the order, kicked a ground ball at first base to open the ninth, and the runner he reprieved came round upon Clement's sacrifice fly to undo a 2-1 lead and force extra innings. Whereupon Rice strode to the plate in the tenth and hit the two-run homer — his three-and-thirtieth — that won the game outright. 'You just gotta have as short of a memory as you possibly can,' said the redeemed. 'Obviously, no one's feeling worse at that point than Benny,' added the manager Boone. 'That's this game. That's being a big leaguer.' The victory wasted nothing of Weathers' seven and a third innings of one-run pitching, and survived ten strikeouts from the Toronto ace Cease, whose two hits allowed across six and a third deserved kinder company. Giménez singled home a run in the last of the tenth to restore the terror before Hill closed the door. New York's three-game skid is ended; the Jays' climb pauses a game from the final chair.

OLSON'S MOONSHOT SALVAGES THE FINALE: BRAVES 5, SONORAN NINE 3

Arizona had twice drawn level by solo homer — Moreno's ninth and the elder Vargas' ninth — and seemed intent on stealing the finale as it had taken the series, when Matt Olson settled matters in the seventh with a three-run blast to center, his six-and-thirtieth of the season, drawing him within a single homer of Schwarber's National League lead. Elder gave six innings of one-run ball, Iglesias recorded his five-and-twentieth save with the tying run at the plate, and the Atlantas — still masters of the East at four-and-seventy wins — avoided the indignity of a home sweep at the hands of a wild-card rival. The Snakes, for their part, leave Georgia with the series in their luggage and a date in Boston tonight, one game removed from the National's open chairs.

FIVE IN THE THIRD AND THE BUCS BITE BACK: PIRATES 8, CRIMSON HOSE 3

A day after Gray's masterpiece, Boston's bats returned to their August slumber — five hits, thirteen strikeouts — while Pittsburgh feasted early: two in the first and five in the third, Reynolds twice singling or doubling home runners for two runs batted in, Lowe driving in two more, and Nick Yorke — recalled from Indianapolis that very morning — announcing his return with three runs batted in. Wong's three-run homer in the fifth was the whole of the Boston reply. The victory went, in the modern bookkeeping, to Yates, his first of the season against five defeats; the Smoky City men now turn to greet Detroit, due at their park this very evening.

THE BROOM COMES OUT AT COMERICA: SOUTH SIDERS 7, MOTOR CITY NINE 5

Twice behind — three-nought early, four-one in the fifth — Chicago simply kept swinging until the arithmetic relented, as this club has done all season. Romo began the recovery with a two-run homer, C. Montgomery singled home the equalizer, Murakami untied it in the seventh with his eight-and-twentieth homer — a two-run thunderclap — and M. Vargas matched that homer total with an insurance blast in the ninth. The sweep runs the division lead to five and a half games, the South Siders' fattest cushion since the final day of 2021, the year of their last crown. 'These guys are tired and beat up and they just keep playing,' said the manager Venable, declining for the third time in three days to call it a statement. The Detroit manager Hinch made it for him: 'They're never out of it... They're a very good team, and their record reflects it.' For the Bengals — whose freshly summoned Callahan tripled home two — a third straight defeat leaves them a full game from the wild-card chair they held a week ago.

SEVEN INNINGS OF NOTHING, THEN EVERYTHING AT ONCE: GULF STREAM NINE 7, RED STOCKINGS 1

For seven innings the rubber match in Cincinnati was a pitchers' duel of the severest school — Pérez granting two hits and no runs across six for Miami, Lodolo five scoreless frames for the home nine — and then the dam gave way all in one direction. Hernández opened the eighth with his eighteenth homer, Conine walked home a second with the sacks full, and the ninth brought the deluge: Ramírez's two-run double and Sanoja's three-run homer, five runs against a bullpen abetted by three Cincinnati errors, two of them charged to De La Cruz. Stephenson's pinch homer was the Queen City's single answer. The Floridians take the series and sit three games from the National's last chair; the Reds must regroup by 1:40 this afternoon, when the Cardinals arrive for two.

THREE HOURS OF RAIN, SIX INNINGS OF NOTHING, FOUR BALLS OVER THE WALL: MISSION NINE 5, GUARDIANS 0

The skies over Cleveland delayed the first pitch three hours and eleven minutes; Casey Mize was worth the wait. In his third start since the deadline conveyance out of Detroit, the right-hander scattered three hits across six scoreless innings for his first National League victory, no Cleveland runner passing second base all day. 'When I got out there, it felt normal,' he shrugged. 'It felt like the game started right on time for me.' The San Diego runs arrived by solo subscription — Rengifo, Sheets, Bowen, and Cronenworth each clearing the fence once, with Bogaerts singling home the fifth — and the Padres claimed the rubber game, drawing level with Philadelphia at seven-and-sixty wins apiece for the National's two open chairs. Cleveland, toasted Saturday for its ten-thousandth victory, was reminded Sunday that the ledger of 2026 keeps its own accounts.

THE FLUSHING NINE FINISH THE SWEEP: METS 4, WASHINGTONS 3

Christian Scott pitched into the seventh inning for the first time since his own elbow was rebuilt by the procedure whose pioneer the game mourned this very day — a quiet tribute, whether the young man intended one or not. Behind two runs after three, he steadied entirely, and the bats did the rest: Torrens' two-run homer and Young's run-scoring double reversed the score in the middle innings, and the relief corps — Senga at the last, his third save inside a week — permitted Washington nothing further. Ortiz homered and Ruiz drove in two for the Nats, whose ninth-inning agonies of Saturday became Sunday's quieter regrets. New York has won nine of twelve, and the once-buried New Yorkers now play the spoiler's part with genuine relish.

DOWN FIVE EARLY, SWEEPERS LATE: PHILS 7, TWIN CITIES NINE 5

Andrew Painter first faced Minnesota as a teenaged marvel in the spring of 2023; his elbow gave way within days, and the surgery that followed cost him three seasons. Sunday, facing those same Twins, he was reminded how long the road back runs: a four-pitch walk to open the game, the bases refilled behind him, and Brooks Lee's two-out grand slam — struck on a hung slider one pitch after Lee had hooked its twin just inches foul — before the first inning was done, with Clemens' homer making it five-nought by the third. Whereupon the Philadelphia offense staged its second comeback in as many days: Arraez chipped one home in a four-run sixth crowned by Bohm's three-run homer — this a day after the man's five-hit evening — and De La Cruz singled home the go-ahead pair in the eighth. Duran closed for his six-and-twentieth save, sealing the club's first sweep since June and a lead of one full game over Arizona in the wild-card table.

THIRTEEN RUNS AMONG THE CELLARS, AND THE ROOKIES FEAST: ROX 13, JINTS 7

The connoisseurs of the draft table were served a banquet by the Bay. San Francisco led seven-to-six after five, whereupon Colorado scored seven unanswered: a run home on a wild pitch, Carrigg struck by a pitch with the bases loaded, Moniak's two-run single — three runs batted in on his day — and Sullivan's three-run homer in the seventh. The curiosity of the box score belongs to Amador, who managed but a single official at-bat yet scored three times and drove in three, his first homer of the season doing the heavy hauling in a four-run second. Devers answered with his five-and-twentieth homer, his thirtieth double, and three runs batted in for the Frisco nine, to no lasting avail. The Mountain men take the series among the season's cellar-dwellers — and in the connoisseur's standings, the ones read bottom-up with an eye on next June's draft, thereby cede precious ground.

THE WHITE ELEPHANTS TRAMPLE TEXAS OUT OF THE CHAIR: ATHLETICS 5, ARLINGTON MEN 2

One day in the wild-card seat, and Texas has already surrendered the furniture. Burger's one-and-twentieth homer staked the visitors early, but the Elephants answered with thirteen hits and three homers of their own: Butler's two-run reply in the second, Gelof's two-run blow in the seventh — charged to Junis, activated from the injured list but a day before — and Tommy White's first of the season in the eighth. Lopez gave six innings of two-run ball, the Texas batsmen struck out twelve times, and the Rangers, at one-and-sixty wins, wake this morning a half-game astern of Baltimore with the Washingtons due at Arlington tomorrow. Some seven thousand souls saw the spoilers work; the spoilers, at least, looked pleased.

ONE HIT, ONE HUNDRED FIFTEEN PITCHES, ONE MAN: ROYAL BLUES 3, SERAPHS 0

The day's finest pitching belonged to Kansas City's Noah Cameron, who went the whole distance at Anaheim and permitted precisely one hit — a single off the bat of Grissom — with a lone walk and eight strikeouts across a hundred and fifteen pitches, the complete-game whitewash rendered in two hours and sixteen minutes. The series thus produced consecutive shutouts pitched in opposite directions: Detmers' 1-0 gem for the Seraphs on Saturday, answered Sunday by a club that keeps its dignity even in the season's basement. Witt Jr. and Massey supplied homers — the fourteenth and eleventh respectively, Massey adding three hits — and Jensen singled home the third. Anaheim's offense for the afternoon: one single, one walk, and the long walk home.

A STUMBLE, A RECOVERY, AND A SERIES CLAIMED IN THE HOUSE OF HORRORS: MARINERS 3, HOUSTON NINE 2

Sunday night at Daikin Park supplied the season's concentrated essence of Seattle baseball. Arozarena opened the evening with his seventeenth homer, Raleigh added his thirteenth, and Woo carried a lead through six — whereupon the eighth inning turned gothic: a pop fly from Altuve that ought to have been routine instead found grass amid a stumble, the bases filled, and Varsho hooked a would-be dagger just foul before Domínguez struck him out to end the terror. 'Only in Houston would something like that happen,' said Raleigh. 'We always play the craziest games here.' Muñoz, two days removed from a five-run cataclysm on this same mound, closed the ninth without incident for his two-and-twentieth save. Peña and Allen homered for the Houston nine, whose grip on the West continues to loosen — two games now over Texas, with the mariners of the Sound but four back and climbing.

The arithmetic desk reports a change of tenancy: the American's final wild-card chair, occupied Saturday by Texas, belongs this morning to Baltimore — one-and-sixty wins, sole possession, no cotenants — with the Rangers a half-game astern, Toronto and Detroit a full game back, Minnesota and Cleveland a game and a half, and Seattle two and a half: seven claimants, and still not one of them at the break-even line. In the National, Philadelphia and San Diego share the two open chairs at seven-and-sixty wins apiece, Arizona one back, Miami three, St. Louis three and a half. This day's card runs to eleven engagements, the idle Brewers having earned their Monday. The bill of fare: Baltimore goes for the four-game sweep at the Trop at 6:05, McClanahan, his back mended, restored to the Tampa rotation expressly to prevent it, opposite Young and his 9-and-3; the doubleheader at Cincinnati opens at 1:40; Sánchez — fifteen victories, a 2.54 figure — takes the ball for Philadelphia against Miami at 6:40; Detroit seeks its footing at Pittsburgh at 7:05; and at 8:05 the city of Chicago closes its streets for the crosstown engagement at Wrigley, South Side against North, Castillo opposite Imanaga. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THREE SWINGS, THREE THUNDERBOLTS, AND THE RECORD BOOK REWRITTEN: BÁEZ HOMERS IN HIS FIRST THREE AT-BATS AT THE DAWN OF HIS CAREER — CARDINALS 8, CUBS 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 39 · Sunday, the Sixteenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THREE SWINGS, THREE THUNDERBOLTS, AND THE RECORD BOOK REWRITTEN: BÁEZ HOMERS IN HIS FIRST THREE AT-BATS AT THE DAWN OF HIS CAREER — CARDINALS 8, CUBS 4

Summoned from Memphis but a day before, the young outfielder greets the first pitch ever thrown to him in the major leagues with a four-hundred-and-forty-nine-foot thunderclap to dead center, adds a second homer his next time up and a third in the sixth — five runs driven in, a standing ovation from the rival faithful, and the first three-homer debut in the whole recorded history of the game

The Herald has chronicled prodigies before, but it has never had occasion to set down what Joshua Báez did at Wrigley Field on Saturday afternoon, for the sufficient reason that in the annals of more than three-and-twenty thousand major leaguers, no man had ever done it. The Cardinals' No. 3 prospect, summoned Friday from Memphis with his four-and-thirty Triple-A home runs, stepped in against the veteran left-hander Matthew Boyd with two out and a man aboard in the first, beheld a fastball at the letters — the first major-league pitch of his life — and dispatched it four hundred and forty-nine feet to dead center, the ball leaving his bat at nearly nine-and-a-hundred miles per hour. His second time up he worked a full count and ripped a changeup down the left-field line, becoming but the second man since 1900 to homer in his first two career at-bats in a single game, joining Bob Nieman of the 1951 Browns. And in the sixth, facing Boyd a third time, he drove a pitch the opposite way to right — 'I had no idea,' he confessed. 'So I just started running, and then I seen that it went over and I was like, this is insane' — and with it went where no ballplayer had gone before: three at-bats, three home runs, in his major-league debut.

By the eighth the entire premises had surrendered to the occasion. The Wrigley crowd — a rival crowd, be it remembered — stood for the rookie's fourth appearance, and the Chicago pitcher Colin Rea was obliged to cup a hand to his ear to hear the signals over the din. Báez lined out to left; the faithful applauded him anyway. 'It's just unreal,' said the young man, who finished three-for-four with five runs driven in. 'For me to not only get a hit, but hit three home runs is just crazy.' His manager Oliver Marmol, asked beforehand what excited him about the newcomer, had answered that the lad's talent 'doesn't quietly whisper — it screams at you'; afterward he ranked the spectacle with watching Pujols strike his seven-hundredth. The starter Michael McGreevy, who contributed six innings in which every run against him crossed unearned, submitted the day's driest verdict: 'I love when history gives me run support.' Boyd, who surrendered all three blows, tipped his cap in the old manner: 'He's a good hitter. He just got the better of me today.'

The supporting particulars: Burleson struck his twentieth homer and drove in two, Jordan added his second, and the eight runs stood comfortably against the reply of Conforto, whose tenth homer figured among three Chicago runs driven in. The Elias scribes note that no man had previously managed a three-homer game earlier than his tenth career contest; Báez required one. He is likewise the first Cardinal to homer upon the first pitch of his career since a pitcher named Adam Wainwright turned the trick in 2006. The ledger gives the affair consequence beyond the poetry: St. Louis, at two-and-sixty wins, stands three and a half games from the National's final wild-card chair, while the Cubs — still holders of the first chair by six full games — see the rubber match arrive this very afternoon.

News Around the League

THE VERDICT FROM TORONTO: GUERRERO TO THE CONCUSSION LIST, AND THE CANADIANS SHUFFLE THE DECK

The morning's report from Ontario, awaited since Friday's collision at third base, arrived and was grim enough: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has been placed upon the seven-day concussion injured list. The club answered with a small mobilization — the left-hander Ricky Tiedemann recalled from Buffalo, the outfielder Daz Cameron selected to the roster — and the skipper John Schneider has installed young Charles McAdoo as the next man up, with results the card below celebrates. 'This definitely feels different than it has for a lot of the year,' Schneider said of his club's late charge, which has now brought seven victories in nine games. 'It feels pretty damn good.' The timing of the injury remains the cruelest part; the standings, as the desk observes below, have rarely been so crowded.

TEN THOUSAND VICTORIES BESIDE THE LAKE

Let the almanac record that Cleveland's franchise, in dismissing San Diego by six runs to one on Saturday, secured the ten-thousandth victory in its history — a summit previously attained, among clubs founded since 1900, only by the Red Sox and the Yankees. 'That's an unbelievable number to get to, and I'm honored to be a part of it,' said the manager Stephen Vogt, whose 2026 edition has supplied rather fewer than its share of the ten thousand — nine wins in seven-and-twenty games since the All-Star pause — but chose the occasion to play the complete brand of baseball its manager has been pleading for all month. The particulars of the milestone conquest are set down upon the card below.

THE TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-MILLION-DOLLAR MAN TAKES A SEAT

In Los Angeles, the management has prescribed rest for Kyle Tucker, the winter's grandest acquisition, who sat Saturday against Milwaukee — his second benching of the week at home. The affliction is geographic and stark: upon the road the man bats .275 with his customary production, but at Dodger Stadium the figure reads .192 with but two home runs in nine-and-fifty games. 'The splits are stark. I don't think we have a reason behind it,' admitted the skipper Dave Roberts, who observed frustration accumulating in a player famous for showing none. Tucker is promised a return to the lineup this day and all three games at Denver besides; his replacement Alex Call, it must be said, delivered two of the club's five hits in the losing cause.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: SKENES HELD BACK, JUDGE PLAYS CATCH, AND DEGROM AWAITS HIS VERDICT

The gravest entry first: Pittsburgh has pushed Paul Skenes from this day's assignment back to Wednesday against Detroit, the management citing rest for a young arm whose fastball has receded from 98.2 miles per hour last season to 96.8 this — though the man himself pleads ordinary weariness rather than injury. 'Everybody's tired. Everybody's grinding, and we just got to keep going,' said Skenes. In the Bronx ledger: Aaron Judge, fractured rib and all, played catch Friday for the first time since the injury, though the bat stays holstered. In Texas they exhale cautiously over Jacob deGrom, whose early exit with triceps fatigue produced an encouraging examination, though his next turn is accounted unlikely. The small print: Philadelphia's Trea Turner fouled a ball off his right knee Saturday and departed; Boston's Masataka Yoshida left with hamstring tightness; Milwaukee's Brice Turang awaits the machine's opinion of his aching knee.

THE ALMANAC AND DEALINGS DESK: A SHORTSTOP FOR CASH, A NATIONAL AUDIENCE, AND SIX WEEKS TO SETTLE IT ALL

Three entries. First, commerce: the Athletics have sold the shortstop Jonathan Ornelas to Milwaukee for plain cash, and so swift was the conveyance that the man appeared in Brewers flannels that very evening — and was charged with an error for his trouble. Second, spectacle: this afternoon's rubber match between the Cardinals and Cubs goes out to the whole nation upon ABC at a quarter past three Eastern, where young Báez will attempt an encore; the wires observe that no man has ever struck more than three home runs across his first two career games, a record now within a single afternoon's reach. Third, the hourglass: the almanac fixes the final day of the regular season at the twenty-seventh of September — six weeks hence, with every wild-card seat still warm.

The Rest of the Card

MCADOO RATTLES THE WALL AND THE TORONTOS KEEP CLIMBING: CANADIANS 4, HIGHLANDERS 1

With Guerrero consigned to the injured list that very morning, his understudy Charles McAdoo supplied the afternoon's decisive blow — a seventh-inning double off the center-field wall at a hundred and seven miles per hour, inches shy of leaving the premises, scoring the go-ahead run — and added an insurance single in the eighth for good measure. 'It really got the offense going,' the young man said, with some understatement. The Yankee starter Cam Schlittler was hard luck itself, one run across five and a third with seven strikeouts, his league-best earned-run figure settling at 2.19; the New York attack managed four hits, Lombard Jr. driving in the only run. Varland struck out three in the ninth for his eight-and-twentieth save. Toronto has won seven of nine and sits half a game from the American's final wild-card chair; the Bronx men have dropped three running.

TEN INNINGS AT THE TROP, AND THE BALTIMORES TAKE ANOTHER FROM THE LEAGUE'S BEST: O'S 4, GULF COAST CLUB 3

For the second consecutive evening Baltimore inconvenienced the American's finest club. Alonso struck his seven-and-twentieth homer and Encarnacion-Strand his fifth, and the visitors carried a lead into the ninth — whereupon Tampa Bay drew level against Kittredge, the fourth save to spill from his hands this season. The tenth restored order: the deciding run crossed against Baker, and Sanders recorded his third save with the tying man aboard. Seymour struck out nine Orioles in six innings and departed unrewarded. The Rays, at four-and-seventy wins, remain the class of the league but have now dropped two straight; Baltimore, winners of two running, sits half a game from the final wild-card chair.

GRAY THROWS SEVEN BLANK FRAMES FOR HIS CAREER-BEST FIFTEENTH: FENWAY MEN 4, CORSAIRS 0

Sonny Gray, six-and-thirty years of age and pitching like the ace Boston lost when Crochet's shoulder failed, scattered six Pittsburgh hits across seven scoreless innings — working for the first time with the newly arrived Rutschman behind the plate — and collected the fifteenth victory of his season, the most of any campaign in his long career. 'We needed length bad. He gave us length,' said the interim skipper Chad Tracy. Abreu supplied the margin with his two-and-twentieth homer and two doubles besides, and the Fenway men added three in the ninth against Weaver to make the arithmetic comfortable. Boston thus arrests a one-and-six skid; the Corsairs, held to six hits by Gray and company, learn they must also do without Skenes this day, as the infirmary column relates.

THE PALE HOSE TAKE THE SECOND FROM DETROIT AND STRETCH THE GAP TO FOUR AND A HALF: WHITE SOX 4, BENGALS 3

Chicago's grip upon the American's Central tightened another half-turn. C. Montgomery drove in two and Benintendi another, twelve hits in all, while the bullpen — Hicks, Taylor, and Hudson, the last for his fifth save — permitted Detroit a single hit over the final three and two-thirds innings after Kay labored through five and a third. Valencia's sixth homer accounted for two Tiger runs and Torres rapped three hits in the losing cause. 'We play 162. Wherever we end up, we end up,' offered Benintendi, the philosopher of a club that has now won two-and-twenty of five-and-thirty against its own division. Detroit, half a game from the final wild-card chair, has dropped the first two of this heavyweight set.

FOUR IN THE EIGHTH AND THE FISH SWIM PAST CINCINNATI: MARLINS 8, REDLEGS 4

The Queen City men led by a run through seven, whereupon the eighth inning fell upon Antone like a wave: four Miami runs, three of them in a third of an inning, the save spilled and the game reversed. Hernández drove in three for the visitors, Marsee and Mack cleared the wall, and fourteen hits were distributed among the Miami order. For Cincinnati, McLain homered, doubled, and stole a base, and Stewart drove in two to draw level with Abrams atop the National's run-batted-in table at one-and-ninety. The Fish thus even the series and stand three games from the final wild-card chair; the Redlegs have surrendered what the getaway day may yet restore.

SEVEN RUNS WITH TWO OUT IN THE FIFTH, AND BOHM RAPS FIVE: QUAKERS 9, NORTH STARS 1

Alec Bohm went five-for-five with three doubles — the first five-hit evening of his life — and Stott detonated the decisive three-run homer in a fifth inning wherein all seven Philadelphia runs crossed with two men down. The Minnesota starter Prielipp walked three straight at the frame's center, including Arraez — the National's leading batsman at .316 — with the sacks full, and Bohm's single through the middle opened the floodgates. Luzardo struck out nine across six and two-thirds for his eleventh victory. The lone shadow upon the evening was Turner's knee, as the infirmary column relates; the Quakers, at six-and-sixty wins, sit in the three-way knot atop the National's wild-card table.

ONE HIT FOR THE FRIARS AS CLEVELAND CLAIMS ITS MILESTONE: LAKE ERIE MEN 6, PADRES 1

The ten-thousandth victory, saluted in the news columns above, was earned in the old Cleveland style. Cantillo permitted San Diego a single hit across six innings, the visitors' lone run scoring upon a double-play ball in the first, and the relief corps allowed no baserunner thereafter. Kwan and Bailey doubled home runs, the convalescing Ramírez doubled, scored, and added a sacrifice fly, and the seventh brought a double-steal of such larcenous chaos that Cronenworth was charged with two errors upon a single play, DeLauter scampering home behind Kwan. 'That felt kind of reminiscent of old Guards Ball,' Kwan grinned. San Diego's six-game winning streak dies at the lakeshore; the Friars remain knotted with Arizona and Philadelphia for the National's two remaining wild-card chairs.

SINGLES, OF ALL THINGS, CARRY THE DAY IN HOUSTON: PUGET SOUND MEN 10, 'STROS 5

A club that has lived and died by the home run — very nearly half of Seattle's season's runs have arrived via the fence, the largest share in the game — assembled fifteen hits of the humbler variety and administered a thorough beating to the West's leaders, one night after losing to them in the cruelest fashion imaginable. Donovan, restored to the leadoff post, singled home three runs; Young drove in four, capping the evening with his fifteenth homer; Robles tripled amid a four-run second whose punctuation was Young sliding home clean between Naylor's legs. Hancock gave seven sturdy innings. Seattle has now beaten Houston eight times in ten meetings this season and sits five back in the West; the Astros' division lead over Texas is down to two games.

ARENADO STRIKES TWICE AND THE DESERT NINE CLAIM THE SERIES AT ATLANTA: D-BACKS 10, TOMAHAWK NINE 3

Nolan Arenado homered twice — his nineteenth and twentieth — and drove in four, Vargas added a homer and three runs batted in, and Eduardo Rodriguez delivered six innings of two-run ball for his twelfth victory as Arizona seized the series from the East's leaders, Atlanta's fourth home series lost this season. The Atlanta reply amounted to Acuña Jr.'s thirteenth homer and precious little else. 'Everybody in that room believes we can tell a really good story, and our journey is very incomplete,' declared the skipper Torey Lovullo, whose club has won two running, taken series from the Dodgers and now the Braves this month, and sits in the three-way tie for the National's last two wild-card chairs.

MISIOROWSKI KEEPS HIS PROMISE AND THE SUDS MEN STRETCH THE LEAD TO TWO: BREWERS 4, ANGELENOS 1

The young man who vowed to throw the great Ohtani a heater and wish him luck was as good as his word and better: Jacob Misiorowski held Los Angeles to a single run across six innings, his earned-run figure settling at a majestic 1.75 with two hundred and ten strikeouts, both figures the National's finest. Contreras and Ortiz supplied the homers, and Ashby — a starter by trade — closed the final two innings for the first save of his season. The Dodger run was manufactured by the benched-no-more brigade: Call singled and came round upon Ohtani's triple. Milwaukee's lead over Los Angeles for the National's best ledger now stands at two full games, with the rubber match this very afternoon — the bill of fare is posted in the desk note below.

DOWN TO THEIR LAST THREE OUTS, THE AMAZINS STRIKE TWICE: METS 5, CAPITAL NINE 4

Washington carried a one-run lead into the ninth at Flushing, whereupon Cruz was set upon for three hits, two runs crossed, and the Metropolitans walked off winners of two straight. Benge's fourteenth homer and Young's two runs batted in had kept the hosts within reach of House, who drove in three of the Washington runs and homered besides. The victory fell to the animated left-hander Jefry Yan, who furnished the evening's comedy in the top of the frame: he leapt into his celebrated strikeout dance a moment before the umpire declined the call, challenged the verdict, lost it, then struck out Nuñez in earnest moments later and danced a second time, unrepentant. 'I didn't want to look bad, so I had to lock back in,' he explained. The Mets have won seven of ten; the Senators go home lamenting the ninth.

THE LONE STAR NINE CLIMB OUT OF AN EARLY HOLE AND INTO THE FINAL CHAIR: RANGERS 5, MACKMEN 3

Bolte's sixth homer, a three-run affair in the second, staked the Athletics to the early advantage, but Texas answered with patience: a run in the fifth, three in the sixth, and a ninth-inning tally for insurance, Langford's fourteenth homer and two runs batted in leading the charge. Gore ground through five and two-thirds for the victory, Junis — activated from the injured list that very day — bridged an inning without incident, and Latz closed the final two frames for his four-and-twentieth save. The victory snaps a four-game Texas skid and, by the morning's arithmetic, leaves the Rangers in possession of the American's final wild-card chair at two games below the break-even line — with five clubs within a single game of their seat.

DETMERS STRIKES OUT ELEVEN AND WASTES NOT A PITCH OF IT: HALOS 1, ROYALS 0

The finest pitching of the day belonged to Anaheim, where Reid Detmers carried a whitewash through eight innings upon two hits, eleven strikeouts, and not a solitary walk, running his season's count to a hundred and seven-and-sixty, fourth in the American. His opposite Dobnak matched zeroes into the sixth, and the game's only run waited upon the eighth: Frazier doubled and Schanuel drove him home. Joyce closed the ninth with two strikeouts for the save. Kansas City's whole offense amounted to two singles and a stolen base; the Halos have won six of ten, which in the season's basement passes for a heater.

SIX IN THE FOURTH AND WEBB WALKS NO ONE: ORANGE AND BLACK 7, MILE HIGH NINE 1

The Bay men avenged Friday's indignity emphatically. Gilbert struck his sixth homer and drove in three runs, the fourth inning yielded six San Francisco tallies in all, Devers doubled — his nine-and-twentieth two-bagger — and drove in another, and Logan Webb did the professional's work: six innings, four hits, one run, seven strikeouts, and not a walk issued. Lorenzen absorbed his eleventh defeat, and Colorado's brief winning streak perishes at three. The two westernmost cellars conclude their series this afternoon, with the draft arithmetic — the connoisseur's pennant race — hanging in the balance.

The arithmetic desk begs the reader's particular attention this morning, for the American's final wild-card chair has become the most contested furniture in baseball: Texas holds it at one-and-sixty wins against three-and-sixty defeats — two games below the waterline — with Toronto, Baltimore, and Detroit each half a game astern, Minnesota and Cleveland a single game back, and Seattle three. Six claimants within a game of the seat, and not one of them above .500. This day's card runs to fifteen engagements, and two command the front row: at Wrigley Field, a quarter past three Eastern and broadcast to the whole nation upon ABC, young Báez seeks his encore in the rubber match, Dobbins opposite Cabrera; and at Dodger Stadium at ten past four, the National's two finest ledgers settle their series, Henderson and his 2.88 for Milwaukee against Skubal and his 2.93 for Los Angeles, the gap between the clubs standing at two games. The early shift offers Weathers against Cease — he of the 2.40, second-best in the American — at Toronto at 1:37, wherein the Canadians may climb further still. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
